speakeroldname: Hon. Barbara McDougall (Minister of State (Privatization and Regulatory Affairs)):
speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of State (Privatization)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, tomorrow is International Women's Day, an occasion which is set aside to honour women everywhere. For Canadians International Women's Day is an affirmation of the vital role which women play in all areas of our society.
We possess in our country a proud tradition of women's activism. At the turn of the century Canada's suffragists
overcame seemingly insurmountable odds to obtain the most basic democratic right, something we now take for granted, the right to vote. They drew collective strength from their organizations, many of which continue to this day. Women s groups were also concerned about special issues, taking on child labour, intemperance, and unsafe labour practices as issues of their own. The healthier and better social environment which we all enjoy today has been largely the result of women's efforts to translate their own vital social concerns into effective reforms.

By seeking remedies to a number of social ills, Canadian women came to the realization that they had to play a more significant role and exert a greater influence in the decision making process and the development of policies.
Some 18 years ago, the famous Royal Commission of Inquiry on the Status of Women made Governments aware of women's determination to play an active and significant role in our society. Today, Mr. Speaker, women in greater number take their rightful place in every scope of activities, because they have proven themselves in the areas of responsibilities they have assumed so far.

I grew up, as did some others in this Chamber today, in what sociologists disparagingly refer to as the flat fifties. But they were already significant signs of change. It was the age of John Diefenbaker-
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of State (Privatization)
speechtext: -who, among other things, appointed Canada's first woman cabinet Minister, the Hon. Ellen Fairclough-
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of State (Privatization)
speechtext:
-who, as you can see, Mr. Speaker, still has a considerable number of fans on this side of the House.
It was also the time of another female politician, a very lively lady named Charlotte Whitton who was the Mayor of Ottawa. She was fascinating but, as I recall, she wore tweeds a lot and she wore shoes with laces. For those of us teenagers who were devout believers in Seventeen magazine, she was not exactly what I wanted to be when I grew up. However, I was absolutely fascinated with her. She was unpredictable, she was uncompromising, she was intimidated, she was unbeatable, and she was never, ever uninteresting, not ever.

March 7, 1988
Statements by Ministers
As I was growing up these women were on their own to a large extent. However, today women are not alone in pursuing their economic objectives or their social and legal equality. Women now have many allies in that quest for equality. The Government is a staunch ally of Canadian women. We have proven that and will continue to prove it.
MO)
As our Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) said last year at the Canadian Advisory Council symposium on the family:
If old prejudices and attitudes die hard, it must be said that Canada is a changing society largely because women are changing it. I look forward to the day when affirmative action programs will no longer be necessary, when equality is taken for granted ... That is why our Government continues, in its commitment to women, to address the need for full equality. The goal of women, the role of Government is to hasten that day.

We have already taken several major steps to make it possible for women to participate fully in the economy. Honourable Members are aware of course of the employment equity programs as well as the federal contract programs; of our efforts to ensure that women can participate equitably in the job training and development programs through the Employment Planning Strategy; of our reform of the pension legislation; of our concrete efforts to enforce the principle of equal pay for equal work; and of our legislation aimed at the enforcement of alimony ordinances.

That is only a partial list of our initiatives on behalf of women. But none of this would have been possible had our Government not taken swift action to renew the economy. There is a very fundamental truth about equality, that is, that genuine equality does not thrive without a sound economic base.
Perhaps nowhere is this seen more clearly than in the Third World where women's daily struggle to feed themselves and feed their families overshadows and overwhelms any concerns with rights and with equality.
In Canada we are fortunate. We know that to make significant progress on the social issues and on issues having to do with women, those that are so important to the achievement of true equality for all Canadians, we must have sound economic policies. A growing and buoyant economy enables every Canadian to contribute her or his full potential to our society. That is what equality is all about.
Sound economic policies permit our Government to address a number of barriers that still limit the choices available to women in pursuing opportunities. One barrier clearly is the lack of affordable quality child care. Women's equality is a paper promise unless women are offered opportunities to actively participate in all of society's endeavours, confident that their children are well cared for.
Our national child care strategy commits our Government to spend $5.4 billion over the next seven years and another $1
billion annually after that to enhance and expand child care services in this country.

The national child care strategy is made up of three major components. A new child care legislation will finance, together with the provinces, the creation of 200,000 new quality day care units in Canada. Two tax measures will offer increased assistance to families with young children. And an assistance fund for special projects in the area of day care will give priority to proposals aimed at improving services and to innovations in this area.
In short, our national day care strategy offers Canadian parents real alternatives to choose what is best for their children.

At the other end of the spectrum we are addressing the situation of elderly women. I was pleased to announce last month with my colleagues, the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) and the Minister of State for Seniors (Mr. Hees), our new seniors initiative. With its commitment of an additional $30 million in funding annually, this initiative will encourage innovative approaches to meet the wide range of needs felt by Canada's seniors, both women and men.
Since this is International Women's Week, I cannot ignore Canada's continued interest in the status of women worldwide. Last August, in Zimbabwe, I represented Canada at a meeting of commonwealth ministers for women's affairs. That was the second such meeting, the first was an adjunct to the Nairobi conference.
Largely through the efforts of Canadian representatives, ministers at that conference adopted a plan of action that directs commonwealth countries to integrate women in all aspects of their work, including training, development and education. At their meeting in Vancouver in October, commonwealth heads of government endorsed the plan of action, setting the stage for co-operative action to enhance the status of women throughout the commonwealth.
Our activities within this particular forum will continue. I am pleased to announce today that Canada will host the third meeting of commonwealth ministers responsible for women's affairs in 1990. This is a significant honour which reflects the reputation we enjoy for our efforts to integrate women's concerns in our national policies and programs.

A major part of our Government's economic and social strategy is to encourage women to deliver their full potential. We feel that women's equality is good for the economy. Our Government wants women to get their fair share. It strives to offer women the possibility of contributing to the economy. For the economy, that means more resources and improved productivity. For society, it is a simple question of social justice. Tomorrow being International Women's Day, we want to recognize the skills and abilities of half of our population.
March 7, 1988



These are not just slogans reserved for occasions like International Women's Day. They are statements of principle that have guided the efforts of our Government since the start of our mandate.
It goes without saying that women have the intelligence, are now getting the education, and certainly have the talent to participate fully in all aspects of our society. Women know the contributions they have made to our country. Our Government also recognizes women's contribution and their potential for more. We will continue to be full partners with women as we move toward our goal of real equality for all our citizens.
Hear, hear!

Madam Speaker, it gives me great pleasure to rise and address the House on behalf of Canadian women on International Women's Day. This is a day for all women from all over the world to celebrate the gains we have made and to help plan our goals for the future.
We come together today to celebrate our achievements, to share our knowledge and experience, and to rally our forces so that we can continue to press ahead toward even greater challenges.
When I look back over the last 20 years I am amazed and overjoyed at the leaps and bounds by which we have made progress. Things are dramatically different for women now than they were then.
Women have an endless amount of choice today. We can go into areas we never would have dreamed possible before. Attitudes and options have changed, and I am deeply grateful to every Canadian who has helped bring us to where we stand today.
This is a day when Canadian women should take stock of what has been accomplished and where they want to go. It is a day to let our Government know what we want and expect from it. Things have changed for the better but we still have a long way to go before we are completely equal competitors in the workforce. We need help from the Government to achieve this.
The Government has made many promises to women and has claimed to be on the side of women in Canada. I would like to take this opportunity to remind the Government of the commitment it made to 52 per cent of the country's population. However, first I would like to look at what women are doing today and how they are living.
The notion of the Canadian family has completely changed. Sixty per cent of all mothers with young children work fulltime. In 60 per cent of all families, both parents must work to afford an adequate life-style for their children. The majority of women today find themselves balancing heavy domestic responsibility and work. The cost of raising children is
Statements by Ministers
becoming increasingly onerous. The cost of education alone for a child from zero to 18 years is $106,000 today. A couple with children must earn $6,000 more each year to have the same saving ability as couples without children. The cost of full-time receipted child care is a minimum $5,000 a year per child.

And what about single parent families? How can they afford these services? We must remember that 72 per cent of single parent families are headed by women, and that half of these women earn less than $10,000 a year.
It is not surprising they have such low incomes, when we consider that the majority, that is, 72 per cent of part-time workers are women, and we see that part-time workers receive no pension benefits or annual leave or sick leave. When we see that the majority of the unemployed are women and that women still tend to be in job ghettos, in other words, earn 63 per cent of what men are earning, I think it is high time an employment equity policy was introduced to do something about this very basic problem.
What do these statistics tell us, Madam Speaker? They tell us that the role of women and the role of the family has changed, and that although women have more choices then they had before, there is still a lot to be done. Many women are still relegated to occupational ghettos, are poorly paid and receive no social benefits. Many women have to support a family on an income that is below the poverty line. Is it so surprising we have a birth rate of only 1.7 per cent? Is it so surprising that parents decide to have fewer children because they cannot afford more and because our society does not provide them with the support services they need to raise happy, healthy children?
As a society in this country, we claim to believe in equality. We support the principle that women must have the same opportunities as men. How can we expect to achieve equality if we do not help women who carry the heavy domestic burden that is traditionally theirs? What will happen to Canadian families if we continue to expect every woman who works both in the home and outside the home to be a superwoman, able to carry on her career and raise her children without any trouble? Pious promises are not enough, Madam Speaker. We must act now.

Prime Minister Mulroney once said that for many women child care is the key to future equality. I agree with him. Women will never be able to participate fully in the job market if they cannot find high quality affordable child care for their children. The Conservative Government came out with its national strategy on child care in December 1987. Unfortunately, it seems to have overlooked two key issues in child care, the need for immediate spaces and the need for quality.
The Government allocated $3 billion to federal-provincial cost sharing programs with the aim of creating 200,000 new child care spaces. Right now only 10 per cent of eligible

March 7, 1988
Statements by Ministers
children under 13 years of age can find places in child care. There is an immediate need for over one million places. The Government is not meeting one quarter of this demand.
These 200,000 spaces will only be created once the federal and provincial Governments have completed negotiations. When will this be, next year? In two years? Canadian women cannot wait that long. Canadian children cannot wait any longer, either. There is no guarantee of quality in child care because the Government set no national standards. There are no standards set for training child care workers or licensing proper facilities. The Government is going to give away money to the provinces without any system of monitoring how that money is spent.
Instead of creating affordable child care spaces, the Government has put S2.3 billion into new tax deductions. That means that if one can afford to pay $5,000 a year for child care, one can now get $4,000 back in deductions. If one cannot afford to pay $5,000, one cannot get anything back for child care. How is a single mother going to get off welfare if she cannot afford child care and, therefore, cannot go out and work?
Canadian women need immediate funds from the Government to create new child care spaces now. Every province should be complying with nationally set standards of quality and affordability. We need money put into programs for latchkey children, for longer parental leave at birth, for day care at night, for quality day care training and not for regressive tax deductions. This is an issue of extreme importance for Canadian women and the present Government has bypassed it.

The Government has also promised to promote employment equity and make it easier for women to enter non-traditional job sectors. We all know that women are often segregated in occupational ghettos and are thus unable to move up through the ranks. Measures must be taken to broaden their horizons, increase their skills and change attitudes in the work place.
The Conservative Government has just announced it will spend $8.8 million to achieve this objective. Fine, but $8.8 million to help 51 per cent of our population is peanuts! Does the Government really believe it will make any kind of progress this way?
Federally regulated employers and those who do business with the federal Government must now implement employment equity programs. This means they must try to remove unfair employment barriers and make a special effort to give target group members, including women, access to employment.
Madam Speaker, it is not enough to urge employers to make "a special effort". We need compulsory programs with standards and set quotas for hiring women. Equal pay for equal work should apply to all employees under federal jurisdiction. The Government must agree to grant major
incentives to businesses for setting up programs that will help women move up to senior levels.

However, simply setting up these programs will not meet women's needs. We need adequate training programs for women so they can move out of job ghettos. The Conservative Government has cut spending on job training by 23 per cent since 1985. Under the Canadian Jobs Strategy funds were shifted from the public to the private sector for on the job training. It has been found that employers have favoured men over women as trainees. There are no controls in place to monitor employers or to evaluate the work skills acquired by trainees.
[DOT] (M30)
There is almost no funding in language training to help female immigrants. The Government seems to assume that female immigrants will be provided for by their spouses or will take jobs that do not require language skills. As a result many find themselves doing menial labour with no benefits and no way out.
Some programs under the Canadian Jobs Strategy are targeted at women. To be eligible for most of these programs women must be unemployed anywhere from eight months to three years. Any woman who cannot afford to stay out of work that long cannot profit from these training programs.
Training allowances are still less than minimum wage. How can a woman who supports a family afford to get job training if the Government gives her no financial aid? Unless the training programs change and unless the Government allocates more funds soon many women will have little hope of bettering their economic prospects.
It has been documented that under a free trade agreement many women will lose jobs in the manufacturing and service sectors. Even faced with this threat the Government is still cutting spending on job training.

There is another problem I would like to discuss and which I would like to bring to the attention of the Government, namely new reproductive techniques. We have all heard about surrogate motherhood, sex selection and cloning.

We need to set up a Royal Commission to study the many legal, social and moral questions involved. This is a very serious issue that affects many people in Canada. I hope that the Government will start acting on these issues very soon.

Madam
Speaker, it is a great honour to rise to speak to the issues of Canadian women. I must also say that it is a very humbling experience.
March 7, 1988



Madam Speaker, first I should like to congratulate my colleague the Minister responsible for the status of women for her initiative in the House today. Too seldom are women given priority in traditional political institutions and we have very few opportunities to speak directly to Canadian women. Today is the appropriate occasion to do just that, for International Women's Day highlights their achievements and their contributions to our society.
For centuries now Canadian women have been struggling to deliver their full potential as human beings. Our country's heroines can be found in the history of the Amerindian and Inuit people, among the first European women who came to live in North America, and among all immigrant women who had the courage to settle in a new country and who are still doing so. We must also commend others who fought so that all women would enjoy basic rights: suffragettes, pioneers in various professions, first women elected to Parliament. One of these, of course, was Agnes MacPhail.

New Democrats share Agnes MacPhail's vision of full equality for women, along with her other goals of justice and peace. This is why our approach to the objective of equal participation of women in society is very different from that of the present Government.
The Minister responsible for the status of women has stressed the need for economic equality if women are to have equal opportunities in our society. She stressed the events of the flat 1950s when the Right Hon. John Diefenbaker was the Prime Minister of Canada.
It is also interesting to recognize, as we look at what the accomplishments have been, that our first cabinet Minister, the Hon. Ellen Fairclough, was excluded from discussions of the Cabinet concerning the Steven Truscott case because the Cabinet of the day and the Prime Minister thought that it was not proper for her to be present when such discussions as rape and assault against women were being discussed. I think we can reminisce a bit and celebrate the fact that the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) of today would not exclude his female cabinet Ministers from any discussions of Cabinet. At least I hope that that will not be part of the history of the Government.
As we talk about the accomplishments of women in the House of Commons and in the country it is important that we do not exclude the Hon. Judy LaMarsh who made great strides in decision making and taking responsibilities in major departments, in particular with respect to health care development.
I do not think that women will become equal until they reach economic equality. Yet the Government is attempting to implement a trade policy that will endanger the jobs of so many Canadian people and, in particular, women. Many of these women who are the most vulnerable are immigrant
Statements by Ministers
women and those who are employed in industries that will suffer from the trade deal. These are industries that we have already heard will need major adjustment programs. Yet we have not seen any potential recommendations for such adjustment programs.
Immigrant women are attempting to become full and equal partners in our community. The history of women in the country has been that immigrant women have certainly made a major contribution. Today they are handicapped by federal government policies in employment and language training which ignore their needs.
It has been recognized that women face barriers in employment that impede their abilities to secure well-paying jobs and achieve deserved advancement. This is why several provincial Governments, such as the Province of Manitoba, have introduced pay equity legislation and have not been afraid to identify a budget allocation to implement that legislation. The federal response to these employment inequities has been weak and ineffective. We have yet to see a strong commitment to affirmative action and pay equity by the present Conservative Government.
The Canadian Jobs Strategy mentioned by the Minister has proven to fall short of women's needs. It has excluded many women by requiring them to have been out of work for an extended period of time, by failing to provide adequate child care and, finally, by ghettoizing women in low-skilled occupations. This is certainly not a cause for celebration.

The Minister also praised the national day care strategy, but Canadian women know that it does not give them much choice. Affordable and quality day care services will still be limited and fall somewhat short of the needs of Canadian families. In addition, the Government has done nothing to make it possible for income-earning parents to remain at home for a reasonable period of time after the birth of a child.

Canadian families have asked for a child care policy that will offer them quality, affordable and accessible child care. Instead, the federal Government has opted for tax measures that help the rich and do very little for middle and low-income Canadians. New Democrats know that this strategy does not benefit average Canadians. We will continue to advocate adequate services for our children.
If we do not have standards in a national child care policy then what we are really advocating is low paid jobs for people who look after caring, instead of helping to develop our greatest national resource, that is, our children. In this country we have still not established standards for people who are delivering care to our children, and certainly they are among the poorest paid of any jobs in Canada today.

March 7, 1988
Committee Reports
We all know that women and children constitute the majority of the poor in our country. Older women are expected to survive on meagre incomes, and they are without adequate pensions. All the programs in the world can be announced, but until pensions for women are above the poverty level, those people who have worked hard in our community and in our country to develop it and to look after the children, to build the families and the homes, are being relegated to a life of poverty in their later years. That is not adequate for Canadian women. Instead of announcing new programs, I would hope that the Government would ensure that pensions for older women are certainly above the poverty line.
As one looks at the employment program of the Government, it can be seen that it has identified targets. Yet those targets are only numbers. In reality, the targets are met by allocating women low-paid jobs; traditionally, women are asked to take retraining in secretarial work, hairdressing, and they are not encouraged to go into non-traditional jobs. There is not the child care available to allow those women to take on adequate retraining.
When we talk about economic equality, we must look at every single policy that is brought forward by the Government and make sure that those policies do address the inequities that are happening to women in our society. Women are still earning only 66 cents for every dollar that a man is earning. That is not a case for celebration. Therefore, we must work harder to ensure that those inequities are addressed.
What we do recognize today that is a source of celebration is that the Minister responsible for the status of women is a female cabinet Minister. The Opposition and New Democratic Party do have women who are Members in the House. However, we would be remiss if we did not recognize the fact that women are still very poorly represented in the House of Commons percentagewise compared to the population of women in Canada. I hope that we will continue to work together and cross Party lines to ensure that women do have broader representation.
I hope that the Minister takes into account some of the comments that have been made today. I believe that we are addressing inequities for women that have not been addressed by the present Government. If we are going to have equality for women in Canada we must have economic equality, access to the job market, pensions above the poverty level, and we must ensure that our children are nurtured and cared for in a way that allows women to feel that the great responsibility they have taken over the years is also a responsibility of the Government. As partners we will build strong Canadian families, and the future of Canada will be protected if the Government could put into effect an adequate national child care policy. The one the Government presently has is a sham. Canadian women and children deserve better.
Today we have much to celebrate, but there is much work to do. 1 would hope that together, as Members in this House of
Commons, we will celebrate what women have accomplished and recognize that there is still a long way to go; that as partners, and public legislators, we will focus on that and not try to be defensive of inadequate policies.

speechtext: Madam Speaker, as Chairman of the Legislative Committee on Bill C-67, an Act respecting animal pedigree associations, I have the honour to present the Bill to the House, with amendments, in both official languages.

Madam
Speaker, pursuant to Standing Order 106, it is my honour to present a petition from a number of constituents who feel that the present Government has no mandate from the Canadian people to conclude a free trade deal with the United States. The petitioners feel that the trade deal negotiated threatens the fabric of Canadian political and economic sovereignty since it removes the power of the Canadian Government to effectively control foreign ownership, and it effectively removes the ability of the Government to direct Canadian energy resources in the best interests of Canadian citizens. The petitioners believe that it will work against the ability of the Government to reduce regional disparities.
Therefore, the petitioners are asking Parliament to dissolve to allow the people of Canada the opportunity to accept or reject the trade deal during a national general election.

Speaker, it is my duty and honour to present petitions from 611 British Columbians who are protesting the present process of native land claim negotiations in our province.
In particular, the petitioners request that the Government of Canada pass an Order in Council pursuant to Section 73 of the Indian Act placing all Indian Band fishing by-laws under the authority of the Fisheries Act of Canada, and instruct the federal Nishga claim negotiator, and all other Indian claims negotiators, that Indian land claims are not to be settled by granting fish from the public Fisheries of Canada to the exclusive use of the claimants.

March 7, 1988

subsubtopic: THE PROBLEM OF THE HOMELESS AND SOCIAL HOUSING-REQUEST FOR GOVERNMENT ACTION
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the four petitions I present today bear the signatures of Ontarians in Moose Creek, Maxville, St. Paschal Baylon and Winchester, and Quebecers in Deux-Montagnes and Pointe-Claire. Your petitioners deplore the fact that over 100,000 people were homeless in Canada last year, that an ever growing number of young people, women and entire families do not have a roof over their heads, that the number of affordable housing units is constantly dwindling, and that the Government has yet to do something to solve this problem.
Wherefore the petitioners humbly pray and call upon Parliament to take immediate action to ensure that all Canadians live in adequate and healthy accommodation and that a re-integration program be established to make it easier for these destitute Canadians to regain their place in society.

Madam Speaker, I too wish to present a petition. The petitioners are urging the Government not to proceed with the free trade agreement negotiated, and they urge the Government to call an election on this issue before proceeding.
The petitioners point out what they feel are shortcomings of the trade agreement. They urge that an election be held on this topic.

Madam Speaker, 1 have a petition signed by a large number of constituents who are concerned about the trade agreement. They are concerned that it undermines the very fabric of Canadian political and economic sovereignty by removing the power of the Canadian Government to effectively control foreign ownership, to develop Canadian energy resources in the best interests of Canadians, or to equalize opportunities between regions. The petitioners believe that the trade agreement would deny Canada the policy or freedom to determine its own economic future.
They call upon the Government of Canada to dissolve Parliament and allow the people of Canada the opportunity to accept or reject the proposed trade agreement during a national general election.

Madam Speaker, I have a petition presented by citizens of Canada who point out that the proposed agreement between Canada and the United States removes the power of the Canadian Government to effectively control foreign ownership, removes our power to develop Canadian energy resources in the best
Petitions
interests of Canadians and removes the power to equalize opportunities between regions.
The petition also points out that the agreement failed to secure access to the Canadian market for Canadians which was supposed to be the key objective in the negotiations and it threatens the loss of hundreds of thousands of Canadian jobs.
Therefore, the petitioners call upon the Parliament of Canada to dissolve and permit the people of Canada to speak on this issue.

Madam Speaker, I have the duty and privilege to present a certified correct petition pursuant to Standing Order 106 from citizens of the Province of Ontario who believe that the trade agreement between Canada and the United States will have a fundamental impact on Canada's economic, cultural and political independence and that the agreement implies a loss of jobs in many sectors and regions.
The undersigned request that the Parliament of Canada obtain a clear mandate from the Canadian people through a national debate on the alternatives available to Canada and that this debate result in a national election.

Madam
Speaker, I have the responsibility and honour under Standing Order 106 to register this petition that has been duly certified from citizens of Ontario.
These citizens say that the trade agreement would deny Canada the policy freedom to determine its own economic future and it would undermine our abilities to build a society distinct from that of the United States. The proposed trade agreement not only denies Canadians secure access to the U.S. market, which was the key objective in these negotiations, but threatens the loss of hundreds of thousands of Canadian jobs.
Therefore, these citizens ask that Parliament be dissolved to allow the people of Canada the opportunity to accept or reject the proposed free trade agreement during a national general election.

Madam Speaker, it is my privilege and responsibility to present a duly certified petition from a number of Canadians.
Considering that the Mulroney-Reagan trade agreement will have a fundamental impact on Canada's economic, cultural and political independence and that it implies the loss of jobs, the undersigned request that the Parliament of Canada obtain a clear mandate from the Canadian people through a national debate on the alternatives available to Canada and that this debate result in a national election prior to the signing of any such agreement.

Madam Speaker, it is my duty to present a petition duly certified on behalf of residents of the Province of Ontario who note that the Conservative Government has no mandate from the Canadian

March 7, 1988
Order Paper Questions
people to conclude a free trade agreement with the United States. The Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) promised in the course of the bilateral trade negotiations that Canadian sovereignty would not be compromised whereas, in fact, the resulting agreement will constrain the Government of Canada to act. Secure access has not been obtained and hundreds of thousands of Canadian jobs are threatened by the agreement.
For those reasons, the residents of the Province of Ontario call upon this Parliament to dissolve and to give them an opportunity to reject the trade agreement in a national general election.

Madam Speaker, I rise on a point of order. I wish to advise the House that the Government has no further schedule of speakers. This is a matter which has had exposure to the public and the House since June of last year. There has been a healthy debate in public and in the House and all three Parties have indicated their support for this important Bill. We feel the matter can now proceed to the second reading conclusion so that the Bill can go into committee and be fully examined by Members.
I urge my colleagues to allow the House to put the question as soon as possible.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I hear a Member laughing over there. It is no laughing matter. As a matter of fact, it is the usual practice in this House to share information and to tell us what business will be called today. If the House had been told that the back-up Bill today to Bill C-72 was something else, which we were not, then maybe the Member would have a point.
The question before us right now is a very important one. Seven government Members have spoken in this debate, four Liberal Party Members and three New Democrats. That is hardly a very extensive debate. We have had six hours and some minutes of debate and that is all. The principle of a Bill of such importance to this country, which was tabled last June 25, 1987 and called for debate on February 8, a month ago, then shelved by the Government for a month while some people objected to it publicly, I think requires at this time some clarification from the Government, an indication of what it intends to do.
We have heard all kinds of propositions from the Tory backbench. We have heard about all kinds of amendments that will be proposed from the Tory back-benchers. We are looking forward to hearing them in committee but the basic principle of the Bill is what second reading is all about.
[ Translation]
Madam Speaker, today we maintain that the Prime Minister of the country must say where he stands on this issue. The Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Turner) did so last February 9, and we expect the Party leaders to state their position on this important matter, today if need be.

Madam Speaker, obviously the discussion that we have heard to date on Bill C-72 has been very important. The New Democrats have had three speakers and we would like to have two more presentations today. I do want to indicate very clearly that we are prepared by the end of the day to wrap up this stage, namely, the debate on principle stage. When you look back over the debate that has occurred, the principles of this Bill have been clearly articulated and now we can move to some of the specifics, which is the next stage.
I simply want to say that we are quite prepared to see a vote on this before the day is out.

Madam Speaker, I appreciate the remarks of my colleague from the New Democratic Party.
I want to point out to the House that the Bill was called for debate. We are in no way trying to preclude speakers from the other Parties. As well, I would like to say that there is no question about the Prime Minister's (Mr. Mulroney) commitment to this subject because the Bill stands in his name. We are ready to vote on the principle of the Bill and put it into committee for second reading.
March 7, 1988

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for External Relations
speechtext: I wish to inform the House that because of the ministerial statement, Government Orders will be extended by 39 minutes beginning at one o'clock p.m.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: Madam Speaker, the Hon. Member for Charlevoix (Mr. Hamelin) had the floor. He had used up four of the usual 20 minutes allowed in this debate. I take it for granted that he has chosen not to resume his remarks, that the Opposition should now have the floor, and that alternance between government and opposition Members will continue today.

Madam Speaker, the last time I had the occasion in the Chamber to speak on the issue of language was in 1984. At that time, I presented on behalf of the then Government a resolution dealing with a solution to the very serious and painful experience of Manitoba as it was trying to realize its own language issues. By way of comment, I should say that my introduction was immediately followed by the words of the newly-minted Leader of the Opposition of the time who gave what I consider to be one of the finest addresses he has made in this House. I am only sorry that he is not making himself available today to give similar testimony on behalf of such an important issue.
At that time, it was very crucial for the House to assert the national interest, the public interest, in my province, one of the western provinces. There were at the time a number of voices being heard from western Canada, voices of hatred, voices of extremism, voices of terrible and awful prejudice. These voices tended to cloud the issue. I believe that it was a fine moment when members of all Parties clearly expressed their support for the Manitoba Government's efforts to find an acceptable way of implementing its responsibility to ensure the protection of minority language rights in that province.
In some ways, we have a reflection of that same kind of debate today. Once again, we have been presented with a fundamental responsibility on behalf of all Canadians to assert one of the fundamental elements of Canadian society. Once again, we are hearing an echo of those voices that are attempting to fan hatred, distrust and intolerance.
Historically, this Parliament has over many generations had to address itself to three very important axioms of Canadian unity. One is our relationship with the United States. We share a continent with one of the most powerful countries in the world. It has always been one of the most sacred trusts of this Parliament to ensure that that relationship was designed in a way that would ensure the integrity and independence of a Canadian society against the incredibly powerful pull of the other country.
A second axiom has been to deal with the centrifugal pull of the regions, the way in which there has always been a move
Official Languages Act
toward fragmentation, a pulling away from the centre. Again, it has been this Chamber which has had to express itself on behalf of a notion of one Canada. We have tried to build institutions, practices and programs that would hold Canada together.
On those two counts, the present Government has not played fairly with Canada. 1 have been most critical of it, particularly on the first question. The Government has forgotten the need to ensure integrity and independence and the need to ensure that there is a strong, effective national Government able to represent all Canadians.
The third axiom has been the delicate and sensitive relationship between French and English, the need to maintain a balance of languages. On that count, I believe that the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and those in his Government have served and expressed the interests of Canada. They have not forgotten the historical lessons, nor have they attempted in any way to alter what has been a very important responsibility and obligation of this Chamber which represents the entire country. However, there are those within those ranks who disagree. That is one of the reasons why we must maintain this debate.
We must ensure that that minority within the government ranks is not given the credence and credibility it sometimes seeks to attain. That is why it is important for me as a western Member of Parliament who comes from a western province to clearly assert my support for this legislation and to say very clearly that those from my province who have spoken against this issue as Members of Parliament or as others do not speak for the majority of the people of the Province of Manitoba. It is important to understand that, so that those in the rest of Canada-

-particularly in regions of Canada where French is spoken, like New Brunswick, Quebec and other areas of the country, to understand that some people in western Canada strongly support this initiative and the Bill we are considering today. Most western Canadians endorse this measure. There is no minority voice, the voice of prejudice which represents the attitudes and views of western Canadians.

That is why it is essential that we examine clearly what is being said and what successes we have had. It is so unfortunate that there are those among us who try to dredge up the old skeletons of history, who reach back into the chamber of horrors of the past and try to pull out old political shibboleths that no longer make sense.
The successes and achievements of this country have been unique. Think how many other countries in the world are torn apart in the most divisive, fratricidal conflicts. Places like Sri Lanka, Ireland and Lebanon have been sheared, dividing families, communities and neighbourhoods over matters of language and culture. Yet we in Canada have found answers,

March 7, 1988
Official Languages Act
sometimes in an awkward way, sometimes in a divisive way, but we have found answers that have allowed us to maintain a sense of community and to overcome those kinds of divisions. That is a unique achievement.
That achievement has been particularly important in western Canada because the experience and presence of the French language is not strong. Statistically, the languages of origin of many of the people of the West are perhaps German, Ukrainian or Italian. Yet in the last 20 years or so, western Canadians have clearly come to see that this is not a regional issue or a parochial issue, it is a Canadian issue. Therefore, they have been prepared to support and work at the implementation and the advancement of language rights, French and English, right across the country.
The Government to which I belonged enacted the Official Languages Act of 1969. At that time, there was a clear distinction made that the protection and enhancement of the official languages was in no way a qualification of the multicultural fact of Canada. The two could live side by side because in fact, when talking about language rights, we were talking about individual rights, not group rights. Individual rights are the rights of Canadians. Of course, the entrenchment of those rights in the Charter of Rights of 1982 made them a part of the fundamental law of the land.
Mistakes are made at times. I refer with some trepidation to the Meech Lake Accord which advances the concept that we are now establishing group rights in Canada, that rights are established according to one's collectivity, according to the group to which one belongs, not according to the fact that one is an individual who happens to speak French or English. That in itself must be looked at as a trend to be treated with some wariness. As long as we were able to assert the principle of language rights as individual rights it did not damage or begin to infringe upon the concept of cultural rights as we have come to understand them and use them in this country. I believe that that has been one of the successful formulas which has resulted in the majority of western Canadians supporting and promoting the enhancement and protection of language rights across Canada as a Canadian issue. If we find ourselves straying from that very successful formula of ensuring individual rights we could be opening up an avenue of further dispute and conflict.
Flowever, this Bill does not do that. This Bill is very much within the tradition of asserting, before the courts, in the provision of services, and in the use of language within the federal apparatus, that French and English have equal status and are to be used equally by all Canadians regardless of what their mother tongue might be. This Bill is very much in keeping with the precedent, the body of law, and the judgment of past Parliaments.
The view which I am trying to express was well put in part in an editorial in the Winnipeg Free Press. That is not usually
my favourite source of quotation, for a variety of reasons, but I think that on this issue they got it right. It reads:
The anti-bilingual group could have proposed changes that would arouse interest outside their own ranks and would stand some chance of being adopted. They chose not to. They chose to propose a policy so blatantly antiFrench, so remote from policy that all federal Parliaments have endorsed ... that they knew it had no chance of arousing interest among other MPs. That is not policy-making. That is posturing to arouse and delight ethnic prejudice.
Playing to communal hatreds is an easy, sleazy game played usually by politicians and demagogues of the lowest type.
The editorial goes on to talk about the fact that it is so easy to arouse fear among people, as I am sure all of us in this Chamber have seen. Parents in my riding ask whether this means that their children will be denied promotion and advancement in the Public Service of Canada. That, of course, is not the case, but that is the fear which is aroused by the initiatives being taken by my colleague who represents the constituency next to mine. That kind of distortion, when not clearly counted, can lead to the misunderstandings and fears which are expressed. Civil servants in a Crown corporation in Winnipeg have asked me whether further advancement will be based upon one's capacity in French and English. Of course, there is nothing in Bill C-72 which would provide any bias one way or the other. However, the fears which have been expressed give credence and impetus to those fears and concerns.
I would hope that Members of this House would use this time in this Chamber to counter that kind of demagoguery and appeal to hatred because, as the Winnipeg Free Press says, that is the easy, sleazy game played by politicians of the lowest type. I think that is the proper definition of it.
Our position on this Bill has been very clear. The Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Turner) stated it effectively and my colleague, the Member for Ottawa-Vanier (Mr. Gauthier), has been perhaps the most outstanding defender and advocate of it in this House over the last several years. It is incumbent upon the rest of us not only to adopt the official position but to try to speak, as I am trying to do today, from our own regions and our own communities. We must plead with those who have aroused so much antagonism, resentment, and reaction to this Bill to cease and desist. They are not helping the country. They are not advancing the public interest in any demonstrable way. They are simply retreating into the past and relying upon an appeal which goes to the roots of our being, but which civilized society has built up institutions, laws, and practices to suppress and restrain.
Our country is facing so many other pressures. There is that pull from the south, that incredible magnetic power which seems to be so attractive to so many Canadians, particularly Members opposite. There is the centrifugal tendency to pull the county apart over various issues, one being the increasing power of provinces and regions to assert their own positions, sometimes in total disregard of national interest. If there is one place in the country where that must be fought against, it is here. That is the mandate we accepted as federal Members of
March 7, 1988

Parliament. We must think beyond parochial or provincial boundaries and try to establish laws which will represent all Canadians and will provide guideposts for future Canadians.
One of the finer hours of this House was in February of 1984 when the then Leader of the Opposition, the present Prime Minister, in his first address to this House spoke eloquently and with some understanding of the concerns and fears of western Canadians about language legislation. He clearly spoke for all Canadians when he said that one must not succumb but must in fact educate, enhance, and broaden those concepts. That is the same kind of responsibility which we face today with this legislation. It is the same call for a unified and non-partisan approach. Those of us who represent western constituencies can only suggest as strongly as possible that the minority view which has been expressed from some parts of our region does not reflect that which most people think, believe, or would like to see happen.
I ask my colleagues from western Canada to understand the responsibilities which they bear as Members of this House, to speak for a wider and broader concept and belief which their own Prime Minister, the Leader of the Opposition, the Leader of the NDP, and all three caucuses have adopted. They must ensure that this Bill does not become the source of further controversy, apprehension, or fear among Canadians but, in fact, becomes an accomplishment, a further step toward the unification of this country. If we can approach it in that spirit we will have again done our work well on the fundamental issue of how we keep Canada together.

Madam Speaker, I would like to direct a question to the Hon. member. He was here, as was I, in 1969 when Parliament passed the Official Languages Act. It was passed with a very large majority and a majority of the Members of every political Party represented here. It was brought forward because it was considered by the Government of the day and by the vast majority of the Members of Parliament, to be one method, one means, of helping to keep this country together.
I will support the Bill we are discussing for the same reason. I am certain that a majority of Members of Parliament from all Parties will support the Bill.
As the Hon. Member has said, there are some people in Parliament and outside Parliament who oppose the Bill and who never accepted the idea that this country should recognize the two languages, as declared by Parliament. We are hearing criticism that is very often based on misrepresentation. For instance, the magazine Western Report stated that it will not be long before every public servant in this country will have to know both languages, and that every judge appointed by the federal Government will have to be fluent in both languages in the event that someone in the West or Atlantic Canada insists on having a trial conducted in French.
Official Languages Act
I do not believe that any of these statements are factually correct. I am sure the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry (Mr. Axworthy) and the Member for Winnipeg- Assiniboine (Mr. McKenzie) have received letters and phone calls protesting the Bill, as have I. I called the Public Service Commission office in Winnipeg and was told that there are some 6,900 federal public servants, of which 3.6 per cent are Francophone. After almost 19 years of the Official Languages Act, there is still a very small percentage of Francophones.
The Hon. Member was a cabinet Minister and Minister of Transport for a number of years. Does he have any information like that which was given by the Public Service in Winnipeg about the situation in Winnipeg and western Canada concerning Crown corporations such as the CNR, VIA Rail and Air Canada which employ a large number of people in western Canada?

Madam Speaker, first, let me say that the amendments proposed by the Member who shares representation of part of the City of Winnipeg would set back substantially whatever progress has been made. It would lead to the absurd result in St. Boniface, which is a French speaking area of Manitoba, where civil servants working in that language in that part of Manitoba would not only be unable to use the language of their mother tongue but to speak the language of those whom they are serving. Of course, that concept is perverse in the extreme and turns the whole concept of official languages on its head.
There are certain designated services to the public, such as in the airline industry, where that service at the Winnipeg airport must be available in both French and English at all times so that travellers from across Canada can be understood and served. There has been no particular designation other than in those areas where such services are required.
The phobia that the Western Report and others are trying to instill is not based on fact. Indeed, I suggest that progress has not been made in many of our Crown corporations to properly ensure adequate representation in both French and English. As the Commissioner of Official Languages pointed out, there are still some areas where much work needs to be done. I hope that this legislation will do that and clearly signify that the steps taken by the Charter in 1982 are now the policy and program of the Government of Canada. That would require the managers of our Crown corporations and Public Service departments to be more solicitous and responsible in bringing about further changes.
The requirements under the present Official Languages Act are not to displace English but to ensure the protection of language rights in both languages. That is a principle that we often forget. I hope that answers my colleague.
I believe this is cornerstone legislation that can provide the basis on which to build in the future. That is why it is important it receive the unanimous support of the House.

March 7, 1988
Official Languages Act

Mr. Speaker, I want to make a short comment and then ask the Hon. Member a question. I will have been in legislatures and the House of Commons for 48 years next May. 1 have seen many kinds of Bills come and go. I seldom hear people question the procedures of democracy. We do not know what is in a Bill when it is introduced. Once it has been printed we are given a reasonable time, sometimes a long time, to study the Bill. We then have the right to vote on the principle of the Bill, after which it goes to a committee where changes may be made.
The purpose of sending a Bill to committee is to make changes if they are necessary, to clarify the wording or the intent so that the principle can be followed. It then comes back for report stage where there is another opportunity to determine whether the Bill is in its desired form.
Finally, there is third reading stage where the Bill can be either supported or thrown out.
We must remember that we are in a democracy. As the Hon Member said, the principle of this Bill is bilingualism. That principle was adopted many years ago.
Are you for it now?
Bilingualism has been accepted. My people support it and I support it-
You support it?
Yes.
Well!
What made you think that I did not?
You voted against it in 1973.

That is the trouble, Madam Speaker. Some people try to stir things up to hurt what they are supposed to be supporting. Of course I support bilingualism. Anyone in this country who wants to be fair will want all of our people, unilingual and bilingual, to be treated fairly.
Do you support this Bill?

Madam Speaker, if the Hon. Member leaves all his courtesy and common sense at home he should stay home with them. He will have a chance to make a speech. I do not know why he is questioning the things I am saying, which are straight democratic principles.
Yes or no? One word, yes or no?
You are out of order.

But it is much more revealing, Madam Speaker.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order. The time for questions and comments has actually expired. However, if the House agrees, we will allow the Hon. Member to conclude and give a short time for reply to the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry (Mr. Axworthy).
Agreed.

I will do so rapidly, Madam Speaker. The point I am trying to make is that we go to committee to make changes, if changes are necessary. For instance, in this Bill, the English Part I says "all" judges, any judge. The French part says "a" judge. Consequently, I think some thought that every judge would have to be bilingual. It will be many, many years before everyone in Canada is bilingual. So things like that should be changed.
Surely the Hon. Member would agree that that is why we are going to committee. I am sure that with his experience, he is not going to say we should not make any changes which are sensible and reasonable and are in accord with the thinking of people in western and eastern Canada, of Canada as a whole. The kind of country we want is one in which we can work out our differences, a united country. Some groups in western Canada, and perhaps some groups in eastern Canada, want to separate this country and sever us so we cannot operate as one Canadian country.

I thank you, Madam Speaker, for the courtesy of extending a few minutes. I was afraid for a moment that the Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre (Mr. Cassidy) was going to provide the response, which I would not share.
I certainly have no quarrel with the description by the Hon. Member for Bow River (Mr. Taylor) as to how the House works. In my remarks I was not referring to the kind of technical amendments which would improve the Bill about which he is speaking. I was specifically speaking to the proposals put forward by the Hon. Member for Winnipeg- Assiniboine (Mr. McKenzie) on behalf of a group of members of his Party, I think there are some 15 or so signatures. It states, for example, that the new language Bill should reaffirm the right of Canadians to remain unilingual without prejudice. Simply put, the advancement of the official languages should never be the responsibility of Government. In other words, the amendments being put forward on behalf of those Members are of such Draconian extent, they would totally and completely not only gut the Bill but cause a major crisis and confrontation among Canadians.
It was to those amendments specifically that I was referring and which I found unacceptable. I would hope the Hon. Member for Bow River, in rising to speak, would not associate himself with this particular set of amendments.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
Resuming debate.
March 7, 1988

Madam Speaker, it is an honour and a privilege to take part in this debate. I was born in British Columbia and grew up in Toronto, but I also had a very interesting experience, an important one for Canadians. I not only worked in Montreal but also spent a year at school at the seminary in Quebec City. That is where I learnt French, and it was a rare opportunity for an Englishspeaking Canadian to become thoroughly familiar with the French milieu in Quebec.
Madam Speaker, I am relieved that finally, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), managed to impose a measure of silence on some of the Members in his caucus who want to undermine Bill C-72, and that the Government's commitment to this Bill remains intact. Nevertheless, I am afraid the Conservatives have sent two messages to Canadians, one that they will support bilingualism and the other that they also want to be of some help or give some assurances to those who are opposed to bilingualism, that it is okay, that they have friends in the Conservative Party.
I support Bill C-72, and that is also the position of my Party. Although I know some of my English-speaking constituents, for instance, will be affected by certain problems, since there are bound to be problems when changing a modus operandi that has been in effect since Confederation, we are certainly not going to emphasize those problems. I think these issues are important to all Canadians, and we must not forget that the rights Bill C-72 gives to Francophones are also given to Anglophones.
Madam Speaker, Bill C-72 brings us a step closer towards the full equality of English and French as official languages in Canada. In essence, the legislation contains the basic elements of the 1969 Official Languages Act, while clauses have been added that arise from guarantees contained in the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms and the Canadian Constitution. The Bill also includes practices that came into effect after the 1969 Act was implemented.
A discussion of the principles of Bill C-72 means going straight to the heart of bilingualism and how it has been embodied historically.
Madam Speaker, I am not going to enumerate all the principles of this Bill. I am sure you know them. I support those principles, and I believe they should be implemented, although certain technical amendments are in order. But what worries me-

What I am afraid of is the degree to which certain back-bench Conservatives seem to want to basically gut this Bill. I note that in 1973 there were 16 members of the Conservative Party who were opposed to the resolution which at that point related the application of the principle of bilingualism to the Public Service of Canada. A number of those 16 Members are as
Official Languages Act
strong today in quiet, I suppose suppressed, opposition to this Bill as they were at that time.
It is fortunate that the Conservative Party, by putting forward this Bill, is now lending its official support to the concept of bilingualism, something we have always supported and something which was initiated by a Liberal Government. Nonetheless, I have had the opportunity to look at the proposal for supposed re-evaluation presented by the back-bench committee of the Progressive Conservative Government. As my colleague, the Hon. Member for Ottawa-Vanier (Mr. Gauthier) suggested, this is something that should be taken slowly because it could be indigestible if read inattentively and quickly.
The proposal, to begin with, according to this back-bench committee, which I believe includes the Hon. Member for Bow River (Mr. Taylor), states that all references in the preamble, the purpose statement, and other clauses of the Bill, should be-

Madam Speaker, I rise on a point of order. The Hon. Member is insinuating that I am a part of some backbench committee. That is a lie. Let us straighten that out. Why does he not make his own speech instead of making speeches for Members on this side of House?
I stand corrected and I certainly withdraw that reference.
It is not the first time you have had to withdraw something.
We are pleased he is not a member.

speechtext: I am sure the Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre (Mr. Cassidy) will want to stand corrected and the Hon. Member for Bow River (Mr. Taylor) has, I think, made his point very strongly and in language that is perhaps not very useful in this House.

I would hope the Hon. Member would withdraw the word he used, which I believe is unparliamentary. But I have already stated that I apologize to him and I withdraw the reference and I stand corrected on that particular point.

We sometimes have a problem when Hon. Members make statements and the microphones in front of them are not open because they have not been given the floor by the Chair.
