Members do speak without the microphones being open.

March 7, 1988
Official Languages Act
I do take for granted that the Hon. Member does agree that some language was perhaps too strong for this House. The Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre has withdrawn. The Hon. Member for Bow River has accepted the apology. I think we can get on with debate.

Madam Speaker, I would ask simply that you check the "blues".
May I point out that this back-bench committee stated that all references in the preamble, the purpose statement and other clauses of the Bill to establishing bilingualism as a goal of the Government and in federal institutions and to extending bilingualism to the private sector and to Canadian society generally should be withdrawn. Instead of that Members of this committee proposed that alternative words be placed in the preamble.
They want it to read that, whereas the Government of Canada is committed to preserving the rights and freedoms of the unilingual public whether they speak French or English and without discouraging the efforts of individual Canadians to speak the other official language for the betterment of themselves as individuals and as citizens of Canada.
That proposal, wherever it comes from within the Conservative back-benches, and I do not know who the members of this back-bench committee are, goes directly contrary, not just to Bill C-72 but to the Constitution of Canada which provides that English and French are the official languages of Canada and have equality of status and equal rights and privileges. It goes directly contrary to the Official Languages Act of 1969 which was adopted by all Parties in the House and which states:
The English and French languages are the official languages of Canada for all purposes of the Parliament and Government of Canada, and possess and enjoy equality of status and equal rights-
It goes contrary to the changes to Article 16 of the Constitution Act, 1982, which states:
English and French are the official languages of Canada and have equality of status and equal rights and privileges as to their use in all institutions of the Parliament and government of Canada.
It goes directly contrary to the 1973 statement on the Public Service which was adopted by all Parties.
We are talking about measures which have been supported by all Parties. If there is an element within the Conservative Party that thinks otherwise, then those in it should come forward and let their names be made public. I think that what they are doing is profoundly dangerous to the country and to the historic agreement under which we created a society which is bilingual and multicultural, a society in which all Canadians have the right to recognition of the language in which they want to work.
There were about 15 other proposals. The back-bench committee wanted to gut, to eliminate the power of the
Commissioner of Official Languages. It wanted to eliminate the right of the Federal Court of Canada to enforce Bill C-72. It wanted effectively to gut the whole set of provisions with respect to the languages of work. It suggested that any person working in the Government of Canada should have the right to work in their designated language only without prejudice to their job status in accordance with this part.
As far as I understand it, that means that the back-bench committee is trying to rewrite 20 years of efforts to create a bilingual Public Service by saying that anybody who is bilingual will not be able to communicate with someone who is a superior because that superior will have no obligation under any circumstances to work in other than their official language. In other words, there could be English-speaking Deputy Ministers or French-speaking ADMs and branch directors who would have no obligation at all to communicate with people who respond to them in the language in which they have the right to work.
The committee also proposed that the language of work for the national capital region should be English unless a position, section or department should be designated bilingual or French essential. Imagine how most Canadians would feel if it were stated that the language of work in the national capital should be French unless it had been designated to be English or bilingual by the Governor in Council. We would have had outrage from across the country. Yet back-benchers of the Conservative Party see nothing wrong in having that principle go in the other direction.

Madam Speaker, it is also suggested that English should be the language of work for components of the Canadian Armed Forces that are directly or indirectly involved in combat. Are we really going to tell members of the Vandoos and other regiments that they will have to learn English if they want to be able to work in the Canadian Armed Forces? I find that intolerable, Madam Speaker. It is like telling someone from British Columbia who wants to become a member of the Canadian Armed Forces that he will first have to learn French.
Finally, Madam Speaker, these back-benchers are suggesting that the primacy of Bill C-72, proposed in this legislation and, although it did not exist before, nevertheless necessary to ensure the principle of bilingualism is truly applied, be struck from the Bill.
Madam Speaker, I would like to mention a specific problem, but before I do, since we have several language teachers with us here in the House, I would like to try and put the situation into perspective by quoting certain figures that reveal to what extent Canadians are involved in this question.

At the present time in the Public Service of Canada 60 per cent of the jobs are designated English essential and 28 per cent are designated bilingual. Seven per cent are designated
March 7, 1988

French essential while 5 per cent are designated either French or English. Therefore English-speaking Canadians without learning a word of French now have access to 65 per cent of the total number of Public Service jobs as opposed to 12 per cent of unilingual French-speaking Canadians who have access to those jobs that are either French essential or designated either French or English. With the increasing percentage of English-speaking Canadians learning the second official language through immersion, for example, Anglophones who have become bilingual, if the current designation remains the same, will have access to 93 per cent of all federal government jobs.
It is therefore difficult to contend that the official language policy is an instrument which prevents English-speaking Canadians from having access to the Public Service. Indeed, it may very well become a tool which will facilitate access to the federal Public Service by Canadians whose first official language is English provided they make the commitment to bilingualism by learning the second official language, French.
I want to point out in particular that the suggestion that somehow French is being pushed down the throats of people in Alberta, western Canada or in other parts of the country is ridiculous. For example, in Manitoba, only 5.5 per cent of the federal government jobs in that province have been designated bilingual while the remaining 94 per cent are English-only positions.
It is interesting that of those 547 bilingual positions in Manitoba 228, or 42 per cent, are occupied by individuals whose first language is English but who have since become bilingual. This illustrates how the challenge of bilingualism is being met very successfully by English-speaking Canadians across the country and in this particular instance in Manitoba.
The two major bilingual districts in the country are the national capital region and Montreal. If one travels outside this area and looks at the situation they will see that in western Canada as a whole out of 50,000 federal government employees only 1,300 positions are bilingual and 63 per cent of those positions are occupied by Anglophones. In Ontario, outside the national capital region, there were 2,613 bilingual positions out of 35,000 public employees. Some 60 per cent of those positions in Ontario outside the national capital region were occupied by Anglophones who have become bilingual. In Ontario, outside the national capital region, there were 1,700 federal government positions occupied by Francophones which represented 4.8 per cent of the total. It is not that great. It is interesting that in western Canada there are three positions designated French essential. Of those three jobs two are currently held by Anglophones. The 18 French essential positions in Ontario are currently held by Francophones.
In Atlantic Canada there were approximately 20,990 federal government positions in Newfoundland, Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island. Of those positions 1,086 were bilingual and two-thirds were held by Anglophones. In New Brunswick, which is officially bilingual, there were about 7,500 federal
Official Languages Act
government positions. About 2,400 were designated bilingual. It is interesting to note that more than one-third of those bilingual positions were held by Anglophones. In other words, the suggestion that Anglophones are being excluded from bilingual positions does not square with the facts at all.

Madam Speaker, I would now like to deal with the implementation aspect of the Official Languages Bill. Perhaps you could let me know how much time I have left after the remarks of the Hon. Member for Bow River (Mr. Taylor).
Last week, I had a chance to meet a number of language teachers, some of whom are in the House today. They are involved in a labour dispute with the Government or, more specifically, with Treasury Board. Now why is this significant? It is because in Bill C-72 Treasury Board is designated as the agent responsible for the administration and implementation of bilingualism in the federal Government. Among other things, Treasury Board is to submit an annual report to Parliament on the implementation of bilingualism in the Public Service.
Madam Speaker, today, we have a big problem. The big problem is that our language teachers, whose work is essential in order to provide for bilingualism in the Public Service of the Government of Canada, are now in a situation where Treasury Board adamantly refuses to listen and is trying to impose very unfair changes in their working conditions.
The situation is that up until September of last year, it was normal that the professors of the official languages, or people teaching official languages in the Government of Canada, taught for approximately 20 hours a week and had a substantial amount of time for preparation. Is that necessary? Yes, it is. Why is it necessary? It is necessary because a great deal of the instruction that they are carrying in the other official language is with officials who have to work with complicated technical subjects. To use their time effectively and teach them effectively then preparation is necessary; for example, in order to be able to deal with a Department of Justice official who needs to know how to work in the other official language for legal drafting, or someone who is a scientist who needs to know technical terms for dealing with environmental issues in the other official language because it happens to be a part of their responsibility. I could extend that to include an economist who needs to know how to communicate with officials of the Government of Quebec or New Brunswick en franqais over very complex or difficult economic issues.
Someone cannot do that and teach 30 or 35 hours a week. Yet that is precisely what the Treasury Board is asking of the language professors. What the Treasury Board is saying is that those language professors will have to teach as much as 37 hours a week with no time for preparation or marking.

March 7, 1988
Official Languages Act

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: The Parliamentary Secretary, on a point of order.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I think we are discussing a very important Bill, Bill C-72 on official languages, and I think the Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre (Mr. Cassidy) is discussing another measure that concerns language teachers, a measure that comes from Treasury Board. I think it would be more appropriate for the Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre to discuss the contents of the Official Languages Bill.

Madam Speaker, my hon. friend is saying we should talk about official languages and bilingualism in the abstract, without getting specific. I am all for discussing principles, and we support the principle, but we also want to look at how this Government is practising its principles. In this instance, I am talking about language teachers who give courses for Francophones who want to learn English and who have to learn English to remain in a bilingual position, and for Anglophones who need French to be able to function. The Government has now changed their working conditions in such a way that they cannot do a professional job, and as a result, this will deprive public servants of their right and of an opportunity to work in the other official language. How can the Government honour its commitment to bilingualism if there are no teachers to teach the other language? They have been without a contract for eight months. The right of teachers to be guaranteed a certain number of hours to prepare their classes is being ignored, a right that the Government or, more specifically, Treasury Board has refused to recognize in the bargaining process so far.

I wish to conclude by saying in a very strong manner how much I deplore an advertisement that appeared in The Ottawa Citizen and other newspapers recently by the Alliance for the Preservation of English in Canada. The ad states, "Wake up Canada racism runs rampant on Parliament Hill. Proposed Official Languages Act a racist document". I wish that there was some way by which that particular group could be brought before the courts, or in some other way forced to apologize to the people of Canada and to this Parliament for that type of slur on Parliament in trying to bring official bilingualism up to date 20 years after the Act of 1969.
The misinformation, the lies, and the misrepresentations in this particular advertisement are contemptible and should not exist in a free society. I urge all Canadians who look at this to say yes, there may be some contention about how we apply bilingualism, but let us not dispute the principle. Let us work constructively in order to ensure that this society is genuinely committed in act as well as in theory to the principles of bilingualism, and ensure that that is a reality for every Canadian, so that every Canadian of whatever official language group can be served in the language of their choice by the Government that we have in this great country.

The Hon. Member states that he deplores the misstatements of fact which were made in the ad he referred to, and in some of the material that we in western Canada see, for example, in the Western Report.
Does the Hon. Member agree with me that the real feelings of people in western Canada, in cities like Ottawa, and other cities is seen in the thousands of Anglophone parents who arrange for their children to be educated in the French language? Those parents recognize the value of having a knowledge of more than one language, rather than the nonsense espoused by the view contained in that particular advertisement.

It is quite extraordinary if one goes to Whitehorse, Edmonton, Calgary, or Winnipeg, to see the degree to which parents have opted to have their children go into immersion programs and learn French, and the degree to which parents have been pressing the school boards, not only in the major cities of western Canada, but also in smaller communities, to offer education in both official languages.
I represent an area where the question of bilingualism has been a difficult one at times. On the one hand, people have chosen in a very strong way to have their children educated in the other official language. In particular, the Catholic school boards in Ottawa do an excellent job. But it is true that for unilingual civil servants who are 40 or 50 that it has been tough. Changing things is not easy. But at the same time we have to understand that the principle of bilingualism is important. We all want to maintain a country. A country cannot be maintained if we hark back to the 1960s when CN did not make its cheques or its menus available in both official languages, but only in English, depending on where one was.
I mentioned the misrepresentations of the Alliance for the Preservation of English. This advertisement states that the Bill would have the Government "authorized to infiltrate provinces, municipalities, business, labour, and volunteer organizations with its insidious bilingual policy". That is totally untrue. It states that, "All federal judges will have to be fluently bilingual, translations and interpreters are to be eliminated". That is patently and completely untrue. It states that, the Official Languages Commissioner would become "investigator, policeman, prosecutor, witness and judge as and when he chooses". That is completely untrue. Those types of misrepresentation are what I believe can poison relationships between the two official language groups in this country when we should be looking for statesmanship.

Madam Speaker, I appreciated the comments of the Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre (Mr. Cassidy) as he spoke in support of Bill C-72, the re-enactment and revision of the Official Languages Act of 1969. The Hon. Member was commenting in response to a question from the Hon. Member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow) about the way in which English-speaking Canadians across the country have recognized the way in which the
March 7, 1988

country has changed. They are sending their children to French immersion classes to equip them for the new Canada.
Has the Hon. Member seen something of the survey done by the Canadian Facts people a couple of years ago? Could he say something more about the way in which legislation when it responds to a national necessity, which the Official Languages Bill did in 1969, can play its part in changing a country, developing new attitudes and giving us a Canada which is much more sensitive to the realities of French and English in this country than was the case back in the days when even federal Crown corporations could be found quite blind to the reality that there were many Canadians who preferred to speak in French or who were even French unilingual but were neglected?

Madam Speaker, 1 grew up in the 1950s. I was fortunate to become bilingual as a child. It is a real privilege and it is something now which has become much more open to Canadians than it was. I was the only Anglophone in a French speaking college classique in Quebec, totally immersed, and being the only Anglophone indicated how few Anglophones had that particular experience.
I am very much familiar with the degree to which we had two solitudes in Canada up until the end of the 1960s. Yes, I believe we have changed and changed substantially since then. Change is not without difficulty. We see that even today as Quebec struggles with such issues as the question of Bill 101.
I think that after 20 years of worrying about Quebec's future status and whether Quebec would be part of Canada, we now have a constitutional accord in which Quebec agrees that it wants to be a part of Canada. That in itself is a tribute to the foresight of all three Parties in adopting the Official Languages Act in 1969 as one of a number of significant steps to ensuring greater equality for the two language groups and for ensuring that French speaking Canadians were not locked into a linguistic ghetto which excluded them from the rest of Canada.
It is also fair to point out that in 1969 there were problems for French Canadians while in that period of time English Canadians in Quebec, then as now, had a wide range of services in the Province of Quebec, yet French Canadians outside of Quebec did not. To this day there are still problems. Nonetheless, for French Canadians in the other provinces outside of Quebec the situation has improved dramatically over the course of the last 20 years. Education is now available for their children in the language of their choice, a choice which hardly existed back 20 years ago. A number of provinces, including Ontario, albeit with difficulty, and certainly New Brunswick which has become officially bilingual, have recognized the existence of the linguistic minority. These have also been essential building blocks toward the creation of a country which can live with itself and where linguistic groups can live with each other much more happily and constructively
Official Languages Act
and, I hope, permanently than perhaps was the case 20 years ago.

Madam Speaker, this is a Bill that we celebrate in the Official Opposition. We are pleased to see it brought forward. We were anxious during a period of delay and during a controversial period when media reported hesitations and uncertainties. I was hoping that today at the beginning the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) would be on his feet.

I am told he was in the House today, to emphasize his commitment to this Bill and to give us the assurance that it will be passed with its main principles intact and perhaps even strengthened in committee, and that we will soon embark on this second, very important stage in providing for an official languages policy that is fair to all Canadians.

I have thousands and thousands of bilingual Canadians living in my riding of York Centre. But the second language which they speak is not French. The first language is English. The second language could be Italian, it could be Hindi, it could be Urdu, it could be eastern European and it could be Spanish, to a growing degree. The bilingual Canadians of York Centre are, by and large, not English-French speakers but English and something else.
As many of them are new to our country, a question they undoubtedly ask is why is Canada committed to official languages French and English and why not to Ukrainian as a second language or to one of the many, second languages that are spoken in my riding. There is a very good answer to that question, a very important one. It is an answer more and more with which newcomers to our country come into contact and which I believe once understood gives a very wide acceptance and understanding about why French and English are the official languages of Canada. The answer lies in our history. The answer lies in our constitutional arrangements. The answer, I would assert, lies in the soul of our country. More and more I hope Canadians will come not only to accept and understand but to recognize the source of strength that we derive from having two such important historic and widely understood languages as the official languages of our country.
So far as the numbers are concerned, there is no other language group that can claim the numbers that there are of French speaking people in our country. The Ukrainian community which might be third or the German community which might be third is very far behind the Italian community which has, I think, 400,000 Italian Canadians of Italian origin, born in Italy, living in the Metropolitan Toronto region. Even they, with their very large numbers, are far behind the French fact in Canada, the millions and millions of Canadians for whom French is their first language and is still the main language they speak.

March 7, 1988
Official Languages Act
On the numbers question, although you may lift up your head in York Centre and look hard to find a French speaking person, looking across the national scene there is no doubt that French is the predominant, second most frequently used language in Canada. That though is not the whole of the story. The important fact is our constitutional arrangements. We would not have a Canada, a country stretching from sea to sea if a fundamental understanding had not been reached that the official language minority, the English in Quebec, the French living in the rest of the country would have their linguistic rights protected.
That understanding and engagement which was reached back in the 1860s in its original version provided the cement in sufficient quantity to tie together a huge continent north of the United States as one country.
To show how important that cement is, we do not have to look very far back in our history. We have simply to look back to the late 1960s and 1970s when a fear of survival on the part of Francophones mainly living in Quebec was behind a great shaking of the foundations of Canada, the possible risk of us losing our nation, a debate, a campaign, a period of soul searching by the people of Quebec and the rest of us and a commitment to a renewed and strengthened federalism in Canada. It is that renewed and strengthened federalism which provides the latest historic reinforcement of our two official languages of French and English.
Those who have arrived in Canada lately, of whom so many are my constituents, appreciate this country tremendously. It is for them a land of opportunity, and it is an opportunity for us to have them here with their energy, education, resources, muscles and talents, all the things they offer to build our country. It is important for them to recognize, as I think they do, that a life in Canada would not be possible if this were not a bilingual country where French and English were equally respected.
I would like to turn to the Bill, but first I would like to say one more thing about French and English. We are lucky, and we do not appreciate our good fortune, to have these two particular languages as our official languages. It is worth reminding Canadians who are mainly unilingual about the richness and power of the other of our great languages. We do not have the problem a country like Belgium has with part of the population speaking French and the other part speaking Flemish, a language with its own richness but a language with a very small international community behind it.
We do not have the problem of an African country where one of the official languages is Swahili, a language which may well be a rich and interesting one but is one with no written dimension and no literature, spoken by 150,000 or 160,000 people. Yet the exigencies of that country make Swahili an official language and ask others to learn that language. We could handle a challenge like that in Canada, I think, but we
do not have to. We have two rich, full, historic languages which have so much merit that more and more Canadians are learning to speak and use two languages.
Some Canadians who attack the official policy of bilingualism indeed think that we are talking about requiring people to learn to speak both official languages. One can understand why they might think so. They see thousands and thousands of people, particularly young Canadians, making themselves bilingual. They are doing this in parts of Canada where it is hard to find native speakers of the second official language they wish to learn. I am thinking of our western cities and of my own City of Toronto where, until very recently, it was hard to practise French on anyone. High school teachers were themselves teaching a language in which they were not very comfortable, a language they had studied academically but could not really converse or live in. Recently, however, Toronto has become more cosmopolitan and more Canadian in the sense that there are rich resources of the second official language available to those who want to learn it and share it with people who have been speaking it from birth or are very fluent in it.
We have to remind those who oppose this flourishing of bilingual Canadians and who feel threatened by it that that is not fundamental to the official languages policy of Canada. Bilingual people have a lot to celebrate. There are a lot of reasons for wanting to become bilingual, but the official languages policy is, as it happens, precisely the opposite.
The official languages policy ensures that French or English-speaking people ought to be able to live their lives as much as possible only in that one language. It is designed to ensure that those who want to live their lives in French or in English, as much as is reasonably possible depending on the region in which one lives, the profession one has chosen, one's community, and one's relationship with anything that Parliament can control including federal government agencies, should not have to use the other language. Service should be available in the language of one's choice. This is an important point for critics of this Bill to recognize.
We are seeking, if I can put it this way, to protect the unilingualism of the group which does not want to have the federal Government deal with it in the other language. When that is understood, it will become much easier and more realistic for Canadians to accept the advances that are represented in this Bill.
I would like to make another point that I consider to be pretty fundamental. The fact that a Government of Canada, Liberal or Conservative, could bring forward a Bill like this at this time tells us a great deal about the evolution of our country since the first official languages Bill. There are features of this Bill that would not have been realistic as part of the original Bill because we would not have been able to put them into effect. It would not have been realistic, for example, to find in every province at least one judge for every Section 96
March 7, 1988

court who could speak the official minority language of that province.

French-speaking Canadians in our western provinces will be able to be heard before the courts in the language of their choice. That is something new for Canada, the fact that we have that possibility.

I do not think it is off topic to mention that I have complained to the Government about the evolution of the criminal justice system as it pertains to bilingualism. When the Liberals were in power, we made provision for language minority speakers in any province of the country to have the legal right to a trial in their own languages, not just to have interpreters present. We provided that one should be able to be tried in his own language, and that meant that we would need prosecutors, judges and jurors who spoke the second official language. That provision was contained in the criminal law reform brought forward by the former Liberal Government.
In that Bill, we provided for late proclamation of that provision. Some people would ask why we did not proclaim it right away if we were so committed to it. We were committed to it, but if we had proclaimed it right away we would not have been able to try people in every province of Canada. There were not jurors, prosecutors or judges all over the place who could deliver on that provision. It would have been against the interests of justice to have proclaimed it in every province.
We provided for proclamation by the Governor General when the system in each province had reached the point where that type of service could be provided. I think it is disgraceful that with the new Government in office for three years there are still provinces which have not proclaimed that law. In Newfoundland and Alberta where it has not been proclaimed, it is possible to have a complete criminal trial in French, and it has already been done in both provinces. That proves that it can be done, yet those provisions have not been proclaimed. Cases are now being taken to court by French speakers who want to have their right to be tried in French in those provinces. Since the Governments of the provinces have not forthrightly declared the provisions to be in force they are having to argue under the Charter that they are entitled to have their trials completely in the language of their choice.
I am not going to attack the good faith of the Government. As I said, I would like to have heard some members of the government Party reaffirm their commitment today and say that the Bill is moving forward to be sustained in principle and to be implemented. I am assuming that that will happen. I am looking forward to seeing the Bill go to committee. My Party has some points it will want to make. However, I would very much like to have seen a proclamation of the right to trial in the official minority language after all these years that it has been in effect in every province.
Official Languages Act
As a result of this Bill there will be better access to justice in the two languages. There will be ready availability and visibility of bilingual federal services in communications. We can look forward to a recognition of the right of Canadians to work in their own official language in federal institutions in accordance with the linguistic responsibilities of those institutions. There will be a confirmation of the principle of full participation of English-speaking and French-speaking Canadians in federal institutions. I hope there will be substance to the commitment to enhance the vitality of official language minority communities and to promote the official languages in Canadian society.
I was critical that the Meech Lake Accord did not contain a more forthright commitment to protect and promote the official language minority in every province. There is now a great opening for the federal Government to act in connection with the recent Supreme Court of Canada decision in Saskatchewan about the status of French in that province. I hope, expect, and demand that the federal Government act to promote the recognition and enhancement of the French language in that province. That would be one way of showing that within the prerogative of power of the federal Government, and within its responsibilities, there is an openness toward the francophone community and the French language in that province. The federal Government ought to take on the responsibility of standing up for official language minority groups wherever they are in the country.
The Bill also provides for federal co-operation with the provinces and the private and voluntary sectors to provide and extend bilingual services. The suggestion which I just made with regard to Saskatchewan would be well within the spirit of that aspect of the Bill.
I welcome the legislative framework contained within the Bill setting out the powers and co-ordinating roles of the Secretary of State in promoting official languages and providing support to official language minority communities. There is a confirmation of the policy role of the Treasury Board and recognition of its mandate to monitor the implementation of the legislation by federal institutions. There is an enhancement of the role of the Commissioner of Official Languages and as important and perhaps more important than that, the Bill provides judicial recourse so that Canadians of other language expression who feel dissatisfied with the way in which the law is being applied and believe they have a legal grievance can go not only to the Official Languages Commissioner, who will undoubtedly act in his best discretion as he sees it, but also before the courts to make their point. That is a breakthrough which I welcome.
Finally, there is provision for the primacy of the rights and obligations under the official languages Bill over any federal legislation which may appear to conflict.

Madam Speaker, I enjoyed the speech of the Hon. Member very much. He emphasized the fact, with which I agree, that the country will always, or at least for a long

March 7, 1988
Official Languages Act
time, be partly unilingual. The time to learn a language is when you are very young. For many years in Alberta we made the mistake of starting to teach a language in grade nine or ten. That did not work. Today 23,000 boys and girls are learning the second official language in the Province of Alberta. This is encouraged by the Government of Alberta which has put in charge of this program a man who is completely bilingual.
Since there will always be, or at least for many years, people who are not bilingual, would the Hon. Member agree that applications for jobs, appointments to boards, and promotions in the Public Service, including the RCMP and the military, should be primarily based on merit so that there will be no special favours given to either those who are bilingual or those who are unilingual? If such things are based on merit we will get the very best treatment possible in each category. Would the Hon. Member comment on that?

Madam Speaker, of course I agree with that. This gives me an opportunity to talk about some details of the Bill. Clause 38(3), which is the relevant section, preserves the merit principle. It provides that:
Nothing in this section shall be construed as abrogating or derogating from
the principle of selection of personnel according to merit.
Merit has a very well understood meaning and has a lot of experience and decision-making behind it. I am confident about the Public Service Commission's general appreciation of the principle. However, it must also be recognized that if the official languages law is the law of the land, one of the requirements is the ability to provide service to the public in French and English, not everywhere, but in areas where numbers warrant. Also, officials who want to work in the language of their choice must be able to do so and fit within a federal public service environment which can accommodate their wish to work in the official language of their choice.
Therefore, merit is relevant; merit and relevant merit in some cases-certainly not in all, and not even in the majority-will require the person involved to be able to speak both of the official languages. That is understood. It is a set-back for some individuals and that ought to be frankly recognized because it limits the scope within which otherwise meritorious persons would be able to perform their duties. However, it does not eliminate their place in the federal Public Service.
The Member's preliminary point was that there are a number of Canadians who can speak only one official language and probably, he said with some regret, that will always be the case or will be the case for a very long time. I go further than that. I would say that it would be a sign of health in our country, a sign of the freedom of choice that there ought to be, if there are always people in Canada who decide that they want to speak only English or are in a situation in which they only speak English, and others in another part of our country who limit themselves to wanting to speak only the other official language. We do not have in this country the goal of making everyone bilingual. We can certainly celebrate the fact
that there is a choice now and that even the province of the Hon. Member, which has no recent bilingual tradition, although it has an historic bilingual tradition, is making its own bilingual tradition. They are making it in our time through these 28,000 young people and others who will be able to speak French in that part of Canada.
I should have stated earlier that it is worth noting that one of the greatest sources of strength for those who have wanted to learn the other official language has been Radio Canada which has produced and provided French language radio and television throughout the country since the mid 1970s. In my case, I owe a great deal of my bilingualism to Radio Canada. I did not learn to speak French when I was growing up as a student, but learned it as an adult and mature student. Radio Canada and the French language CBC network were very important tools for me to acquire the idiom, the way the language is spoken.
For those who want to live their lives in English and those who want to live their lives in French, let us hope that nothing in the Official Languages Act will ever make it Canadian policy to try to reduce their rights.

Madam Speaker, I have a couple of comments and will then ask the Hon. Member for York Centre (Mr. Kaplan) to expand on one particular section of the Bill. He has studied the Bill carefully and has had some involvement with the spread of judicial services across Canada for persons in the official language minority. He just observed that he would not mind if there were always Canadians who were unilingual. It may be worth noting that the Canadian facts public opinion survey in 1985 authorized by the Commissioner of Official Languages found that 99 per cent of those surveyed in Quebec thought it desirable that a person should know both English and French. I believe the proportion for British Columbia, where one might find the other extreme in opinion, was about 76 per cent who shared the opinion in Quebec.
Therefore, there are many Canadians who believe that certainly young people should be educated in both languages and should be capable of working in the federal Public Service in particular with both language abilities.
One aspect of fear mongering, like that to which my friend, the Member for Ottawa Centre (Mr. Cassidy) alluded, is the attempt to turn the Commissioner of Official Languages himself into a dreadful power. Anyone who believes that would do well to compare Bill C-72 with the Official Languages Act of 1969. The powers of the Commissioner of Official Languages have not been enlarged in this Bill.
Of course, the opportunities for individuals to pursue matters before the Federal Court of Canada and obtain some leverage on the federal Government has certainly taken place. That is worth noting.
March 7, 1988

I see that the time for questions and comments has expired.
I will not have the opportunity to ask about another provision.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Resuming debate.

Madam Speaker, I appreciate this opportunity to make a few comments about Bill C-72. As we have seen in the House, this is a very emotional issue for a number of Members. It is also an emotional issue for people throughout the country.
I attended accountability meetings in my riding two weeks ago. At two of those meetings I met people who had read the recent issue of Western Report. They stood up to ask what is this dreadful new Bill being imposed upon western Canada. I want to reassure them that they will be able to carry on and live good lives.
I do not think the emotions surrounding this issue should surprise us. Bill C-72 deals with the language of work and the language of justice. It deals with the language in which people can obtain Government service. In my riding there are people who felt that they personally have been hurt by the program of bilingualism as it was instituted. They felt that their careers had been red circled by bilingualism. Rightly or wrongly, they have a certain sense of grievance about the whole question of bilingualism. Bill C-72 and bilingualism deal with the fundamental relationship between English speaking and French speaking Canadians. It also deals with the relationship of those who come from another language tradition.
The importance of this issue is evidenced by the fact that we refer to the language we learn as children as our mother tongue. Our thought patterns are conditioned in our mother tongue and it is around those patterns and that first language that we have some very deep seated emotions. This is evident when we consider our attitudes toward people who speak with a different accent or a different dialect of the same language.
We sometimes take a very humorous approach to people who speak with an accent that we regard as strange and are sometimes shocked that other people may believe our accent is strange or somewhat funny. These differences are sometimes the source of humour and sometimes the source of snobbery. Sometimes people are educated out of their original accent, so that some people who go to Oxford ultimately have an accent that is stronger than people who have grown up in that area.
Often there is a deep seated prejudice toward another language. This is usually based on fear that is masked by an attitude of contempt. We as Members of Parliament, who pretend to be leaders in this country, must try to address the fear of people, rather than manipulate it, and deal with it in an intelligent and straightforward manner.
First, I believe it would be helpful if both French and English speaking people recognized that both our language traditions have traditions of linguistic imperialism. Perhaps one of the worst examples for Anglophones is the residential
schools where Indian young people would have their mouths washed out with soap for speaking in their native language. They were told to speak English.
I hope to resume my comments after Question Period, Madam Speaker.

subsubtopic: REINSTATEMENT OF WOMEN ON RESERVES-LACK OF HOUSING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the federal Government is preventing women who recently regained Indian status from getting decent housing on reserves. The ambiguous position of the Conservative Government is forcing native women into unwholesome competition with their own people for one of the basic necessities of life, housing.
About 95,000 people have applied to Ottawa for reinstatement to the reserves across the country and most of them are women. They have applied for housing on reserves because the 1985 legislation, Bill C-31, now allows women and their children to return to the reserves if they so wish.
You will recall, Mr. Speaker, that these women lost their Indian status because they married white men or someone other than a status Indian. However, the problem is that although the Government provided special funding for reserve housing for reinstated women, it did not give band councils clear criteria about how it was to be spent. The result is that money is being spent for general housing needs.

maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES FREE TRADE AGREEMENT-GOVERNMENT'S AGRICULTURAL ASSESSMENT
CANADA-UNITED STATES FREE TRADE AGREEMENT-GOVERNMENT'S AGRICULTURAL ASSESSMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Government has published a very sleek publication entitled: The Canada-i/'.S. Free Trade Agreement and Agriculture-An Assessment which was distributed to Members' offices on Friday. Can the Government explain why this so-called assessment fails to show the value of U.S. agricultural trade to Canada? Why the blank spot on page 11 where it should have appeared? Was the Government afraid the fact that the U.S. has always had the trade advantage in agricultural trade would change the reader's view of the agreement?
Can the Government explain why it chose to leave the impression that poultry imports are to be computed only on the basis of a moving average when the agreement specifically states that there shall first of all be not less than 7.5 per cent of Canadian requirements filled from the U.S.? Why did it neglect that fact? It is not in here.
More than a third of Ontario grape growers and virtually all British Columbia grape growers will be forced out of business according to the data contained in this assessment. Yet we are told that they "face adjustments" but this will "enhance competitiveness". How does being put out of business make one competitive?

subtopic: PRESENCE IN CANADA OF FORMER RHYMER ROUGE MEMBERS
PRESENCE IN CANADA OF FORMER RHYMER ROUGE MEMBERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, recently in a major article, the Toronto Star reported that individuals who belonged to the Khymer Rouge and participated in genocidal acts in Cambodia are residing in Canada as landed immigrants. This is a very serious allegation since the Khymer Rouge were responsible for two million innocent deaths, often using methods which rivalled the Nazis.
Such individuals have no right whatsoever to be allowed to live among civilized people. The Immigration Department and CSIS should immediately commence a full investigation to ascertain if the allegations are true. If it is found that indeed there are Khymer Rouge mass murderers in Canada, they should be charged with crimes against humanity. We must send out a strong message that there is no sanctuary in Canada, nor is there any clemency for this type of action against humanity.

subtopic: FIRE FATALITIES IN FORT ALBANY, ONT.-LACK OF ADEQUATE FIRE PREVENTION FOR SCHOOLCHILDREN
FIRE FATALITIES IN FORT ALBANY, ONT.-LACK OF ADEQUATE FIRE PREVENTION FOR SCHOOLCHILDREN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Friday, March 4, four citizens of Fort Albany, Ontario, a small isolated native community near James Bay, perished in a tragic fire. Delna Edwards, age 21, and her three sons, Kenny, Peter and Jeremy, all died, burned beyond recognition, because the community had no way to fight the fire other than with five-gallon pails. Our heartfelt sympathy goes out to the entire Fort Albany community.
This type of incident should not be occurring in native communities. Ste. Anne's School in the same community provides yet another example of a tragedy waiting to occur. It
March 7, 1988

took repeated warnings by fire inspectors before the Government took action to close the school. The children have now been without educational facilities for a month.
When will the Government realize that it has an obligation to take prompt action to guarantee that all Indian communities across the country are provided with the means to ensure that the safety of their people is not in constant jeopardy? The Government must re-examine its priorities and give Canadian native communities the attention and support they rightly deserve.

subtopic: SITUATION IN GASPE-REQUEST THAT QUOTA BE SECURED WITHIN 200-MILE ZONE
SITUATION IN GASPE-REQUEST THAT QUOTA BE SECURED WITHIN 200-MILE ZONE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Gaspe peninsula once more is faced with a plant shutdown. The Purdel Inc. group decided not to reopen its ground fish line in Riviere-au-Renard, putting some 300 seasonal employees out of work. One of the reasons given by the company is the impossibility to obtain raw materials. It feels a fishing quota within the 200-mile zone would have been a solution to the problem.
You will remember, Mr. Speaker, that in December 1987 fishing industry groups in Quebec were denied access to the 200-mile zone by the Minister of Fisheries and Ocean (Mr. Siddon).
In view of the increasingly sad situation of the fishing industry in Quebec, it was agreed on my request that a meeting would take place in Gaspe within two weeks, in order to regroup the Quebec fishing industry and to resume discussions on the possible access of Quebec to the 200-mile zone. Until a longer-term solution is found I am certain, Mr. Speaker, that this Government will help the people in Riviere-au-Renard overcome that unhappy experience.

subtopic: CANADA HEALTH ACT-CRITICISM OF SYSTEM IN BRITISH COLUMBIA
CANADA HEALTH ACT-CRITICISM OF SYSTEM IN BRITISH COLUMBIA
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, following the Morgentaler decision, predominately male politicians feel burdened by a heavy responsibility to reach a decision which they think is morally right and politically acceptable. Any decision should respect different personal and religious views that are deeply held in a pluristic society but should not impose those views on others.

The Canada Health Act states:
The primary objective of Canadian health care policy is to protect, promote, and to restore the physical and mental well-being of residents of Canada and to facilitate reasonable access to health services without financial or other barriers.
The policy of British Columbia of paying only for abortions when a woman's life is threatened is in direct contravention of the Canada Health Act and only serves to penalize women of low income. It establishes a two-tier health care system, one for the rich and one for the poor. It is also in contradiction with the views of two-thirds of British Columbians, as can be seen in a poll released today in British Columbia. When can we expect the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) to restore equity to the health care system?

subtopic: TRIBUTE TO WORK OF HOPE VOLUNTEER SEARCH AND RESCUE GROUP
TRIBUTE TO WORK OF HOPE VOLUNTEER SEARCH AND RESCUE GROUP
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1988 marks the twenty-fifth year of service of the Hope Volunteer Search and Rescue Group. The 23 members log 4,000 hours of volunteer work a year to train and to search for and rescue victims of mountain, water, and vehicle accidents. This is no small feat when one considers the rugged terrain surrounding the Town of Hope, British Columbia. Of the approximately 40 calls received a year, 38 victims are saved by the efforts of these people.
On February 27 I was pleased to attend the anniversary dinner and dance and to join with the others in honouring Clarence Kolcun for his 25 years of service. He is now the Honorary Director for Life of the Hope Search and Rescue Group. I would like to take this time to thank Barry Gannon, president of the group, his executive and hard-working members, for their dedication and service to the community of Hope. We are very proud of their achievements.

subtopic: VANCOUVER SCHOOL BOARD-PROVISION OF MEALS FOR HUNGRY STUDENTS
VANCOUVER SCHOOL BOARD-PROVISION OF MEALS FOR HUNGRY STUDENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, hungry school children in Vancouver are caught between the bureaucratic regulations of the Canada Assistance Plan and the ideological blindness of the Vander Zalm Government. The Vancouver School Board is currently using reserve funds for an emergency program, feeding about 600 children in 23 schools, but a school board application for help from the Canada Assistance Plan has been denied because the

March 7, 1988
plan can only make money available to the city or province if they participate financially, and not to a school board.
The Social Credit Government refuses to participate because it fears the program will create dependency. Instead, Claude Richmond, the Minister of Social Services, wants teachers to let his Department know the names of hungry children so that their parents can be taught nutrition. We repudiate this hypocrisy which claims that the fundamental problem is not with poverty but with the family.
Next week Vancouver officials will appeal directly to the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp). I urge him to work out a creative solution which will cut through the red tape and ensure that school children in Canada do not go hungry.

subtopic: NICARAGUA-ATTACK BY CONTRA FORCES ON CANADIAN AID PROJECT
NICARAGUA-ATTACK BY CONTRA FORCES ON CANADIAN AID PROJECT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we learned over the weekend that, once again, the Contras attacked a project in Nicaragua in which Canadians were involved. I refer to the Farmers for Peace from Alberta.
There were numerous Nicaraguans captured by the Contras, as well as an American. Fortunately, no Canadians were
captured, but great damage was done to the project, to the equipment, and to the buildings.
It is time once again to call on the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) to condemn American funding to the Contras and to send a strong message to Washington that the Canadian Government does not take lightly this destruction being visited upon Canadian sponsored projects by a group that is funded from Washington.

subtopic: CANADIAN WAR MUSEUM-EXPANSION OF FACILITIES ADVOCATED
CANADIAN WAR MUSEUM-EXPANSION OF FACILITIES ADVOCATED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, a resolution from the Defence Association of Canada focuses attention on what many people are already aware of, that is, that the Canadian War Museum has been grossly neglected as an historical, memorial, military, and research institution because of gross neglect by successive former Governments.
The museum cannot perform its role effectively because it is underfunded, underequipped, and housed in inadequate and insufficient space to fulfil its role as a memorial to those who made the supreme sacrifice in the service of Canada in war and in peace-keeping operations. It is also the focal national institution to record, preserve, and present the military heritage of Canada in peace and war.
I therefore ask the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Beatty) and the Cabinet to initiate action for a major expansion of its facilities, and institute other support programs to ensure that Canadians from every walk of life are made aware of our proud military heritage.

Mr. Speaker, today in Vancouver the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. Siddon) is announcing an important conservation program that will affect all groups of fishermen-sports, native, and commercial.
It is well known in my Province of British Columbia that over the last 10 years the catch and escapement of Chinook, our king salmon, declined by some 75 per cent in the lower Strait of Georgia. The stocks are being overfished. Thus new enhancement and conservation measures must be introduced.
Beginning on April 10 all fishermen will be required to affix conservation tags to Chinook caught in B.C. waters. The

Is this not a clear contradiction of the aims and objectives set forward in the Western Diversification Program? The rhetoric is okay but the cash is not there to back it up.

There was a report last week on the number of women who are now entrepreneurs and how well they are doing, and how well they will do under free trade.
I think for the next century that free trade will see women's economic equality proceed even further than it has done.

subsubtopic: CLOSURE OF MASSEY COMBINES PLANT IN BRANTFORD- RETENTION OF TECHNOLOGY
speechtext:

More than 2,500 people who are either working or are on lay-off are looking to the Government to ensure that their jobs are not lost forever. Canadian men and women want assurances that we will not lose the rotary combine technology that was developed with taxpayers' money, leaving this country without a major producer in this vital area.
Will the Prime Minister assure those workers that the Government will seek out a Canadian buyer that will use that technology to build combines and provide jobs in Brantford?
March 7, 1988

speechtext: When the House rose the Hon. Member for Cowichan-Malahat-The Islands (Mr. Manly) had the floor.

Madam Speaker, just before the House rose for lunch I was pointing out that there is a lot of emotion surrounding the whole subject of language. There is a certain degree of fear, some prejudice and sometimes there are people who attempt to manipulate our fears and prejudices.
I also pointed to what I called linguistic imperialism. Certainly both English and French have been used in an imperialistic way to force themselves upon other peoples around the world. That is generally true of European languages, as I suppose it is of other languages in other parts of the world.
I pointed to the Canadian experience where Indian young people who went to residential schools and spoke their own Indian language were forced to speak English. Their mouths were washed out with soap if they spoke their own Indian language.
Today there is a situation in which many Indian nations are faced with the loss of their languages. Indeed, some have been lost because of that kind of cultural imperialism.
This Bill represents an attempt to do something quite different. We are trying to guarantee the equality of both our official languages.
Everyone recognizes that it is difficult to maintain a language when one is in a minority situation. That is certainly obvious when we consider Canada west of the Ottawa River. The further west one travels, the more difficult it is for francophone communities to maintain their own language. In British Columbia, for example, Maillardville is the only francophone community in that province which still maintains French as the language of the community.
At this time I want to pay tribute to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) for the kind of leadership he has shown in this whole question of language. I wish he had continued to show that leadership today by speaking on this Bill because it would have been helpful if he had spoken. However, he chose not to do so.
March 7, 1988

When he was Leader of the Opposition he showed a degree of leadership and courage in standing up to some Conservatives from Manitoba who were obstructing the process toward getting linguistic justice in Manitoba.
What the Prime Minister is saying through Bill C-72 is that the whole program of bilingualism is not just a Trudeau-Liberal plot that has been foisted upon Canadians by Quebec, but a fundamental recognition of the true linguistic nature of Canada. I give credit to the Prime Minister for taking that approach.
We saw a similar act of leadership by a former leader of the Conservative Opposition, Robert Stanfield, when he refused the candidacy of Leonard Jones because Leonard Jones was taking such an intransigent approach to the whole question of francophone rights. This is not and should not be a partisan matter. It is, however, an area where leadership has and will continue to be needed. That is particularly true in western Canada where there is deep misunderstanding of the French fact.
We must admit that it is not limited to the Conservative Party but is an historic fact that runs deep. For instance, there was the situation in 1890 when Anglophones forming a majority in Manitoba stripped the francophone minority of their historic rights in their own language.
David Lewis, former leader of the NDP and former federal secretary of the old CCF Party, pointed out some of the difficulties in our own historic traditions regarding language. He pointed out that he always had some difficulty getting our previous leaders, including M.J. Caldwell and J.S. Woods-worth, to recognize the importance of linguistic and cultural matters to Quebec. He told the story of Harold Winch, a very distinguished member of the CCF who, in 1955, made an offhand remark that all MPs in the House of Commons should be speaking English. That was a completely outrageous suggestion. It was uttered before the time of simultaneous translation. It caused a furore because it was completely contrary to Party policy. However, it was the type of remark that western Canadians were inclined to make in the House of Commons. That took place over 30 years ago, and we have made progress since then. However, there are some people who are still rooted in those old fears and prejudices. I think it is incumbent upon the Government to give some real leadership in this matter, not only in terms of bringing this Bill forward and ensuring it gets through the House, but in addressing the real fears some people have, fears which some people are attempting to manipulate in what I consider to be an unscrupulous way.
It is on that basis that I welcomed the letter that was put into the Western Report by 10 western cabinet Ministers. I think that is important. I think it would also be important if the Prime Minister had spoken in this debate. I think it would have been important if more of the back-benchers from

speechtext: Are there any more questions or comments? Resuming debate.

Madam Speaker, I do not believe there is anyone in this House who disagrees with the main principle of this Bill, which is that Canadians, in terms of the Constitution of Canada, where there is significant demand, will be able to get services in the official language of their choice. I do not think there is any disagreement with that at all. But there is another principle contained in the Bill that in fact has nothing to do with official languages and has everything to do with constitutional changes as they affect the northern territories. I want to address this very briefly.
This principle is contained in Clause 90 of the Bill which states as follows:
The ordinance entitled the Official Languages Act, made on June 28, 1984
by the Commissioner in Council, as amended on June 26, 1986, may be
amended or repealed by the Commissioner in Council only if the amendment
or repeal is concurred in by Parliament through an amendment to this Act.
Of course, the Official Languages Act referred to here is the Official Languages Act of the Northwest Territories, a statute passed by the Legislative Assembly of the Northwest Territories.
The inclusion of this principle in the Bill is adding insult to the Meech Lake injury. It says in effect that the elected representatives of the people of the territories, at the provincial-type level, are not to be trusted, that Ottawa in some way has to maintain control, that the apron strings will remain tied.
There is no precedent in the Northwest Territories Act or any of the Acts establishing provinces where this type of control is to be maintained by the Parliament of Canada. In fact, in my opinion, and in the opinion of the people I represent, it is completely unnecessary and, coming as it does after the Meech Lake agreement in which the territories were treated so badly, it cannot fail to elicit this deep feeling on the part of my constituents.

March 7, 1988
Official Languages Act
If one examines the language laws in the Northwest Territories, one will find that we have probably the most progressive language law in the whole of Canada. Not only does the Act respect English and French as official languages, but it also respects the many indigenous languages spoken in the Territories which were spoken there probably thousands of years before ever a word of English or French was uttered on this continent. The people who speak those languages do not want to lose them. They are faithful to those languages. They feel the same way about their languages as the people in Quebec undoubtedly feel about the French language.
Much work has been done in the territories with respect to the extension of French language services to the small French speaking minority there. We would have to thank the Secretary of State of Canada (Mr. Crombie) for making funds available so that those services can be extended.
The history of Clause 90 goes back to the Joyal-Nerysoo Agreement of 1984. At that time Serge Joyal was the Secretary of State for Canada, and I suspect this was a rather unequal treaty. It is my suspicion that it was forced on Richard Nerysoo, who was then the Government Leader in the territories. It was done at a time when funds were to be made available to the territories for the provision of these French services as well as services in indigenous languages.
The agreement specified that Clause 90 as it now reads be applied to a Bill which was then entitled Bill C-25. It was the official languages Bill-not unlike the Bill we have before us today-which was to have been brought forward by the Liberal Government of the day but, for some reason or other, it died on the Order Paper.
Whatever the situation was in 1984, it certainly does not exist today. Clause 90 is redundant, superfluous and unnecessary. If for some remote reason, and I cannot foresee it happening, the territories wanted to amend their Official Languages Act in a way which took away the rights of Frenchspeaking people-and I do not think this would happen-there are various recourses available to the federal Government to deal with this situation. It is not necessary to put Clause 90 in the Bill. Federal authorities can instruct the Commissioner of the Territories to refuse consent to any amendment to the Official Languages Act of the Northwest Territories. Federal authorities retain the power of disallowance. It can disallow any territorial legislation. Over and above that, it has the power to enact overriding legislation should it so choose. Therefore, Clause 90 is not necessary at all.
On February 17, the Legislative Assembly of the Northwest Territories, feeling as strongly about this issue as I do, adopted the following resolution:
Whereas the people of the Northwest Territories and the Legislative Assembly of the Northwest Territories have in recent years taken large steps towards the achievement of responsible government;
And whereas there is presently, before the Parliament of Canada, a federal Bill which provides for a reduction in the legislative authority of the Legislative Assembly of the N.W.T.;
Therefore, be it resolved:
-that this Legislative Assembly declare its strong opposition, through the
Speaker, to the enactment of Clause 90 of Federal Bill C-72 presently before
the Parliament of Canada, which clause reduces the legislative authority of
this Assembly.
I would like to record my thanks to two Members of the House of Commons in particular who have spoken on this issue already. One, of course, is the Hon. Member for Cochrane- Superior (Mr. Penner) representing the Liberal Party who is in the House this afternoon. The other is the Hon. Member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Keeper) of the New Democratic Party.
Those of us who are familiar with northern issues realize that this is not a Party issue. Rather, it is one that acts against the interests of the territories eventually becoming a province in their own right. Hopefully, that is something that we are all agreed upon regardless of our Party persuasions.
I am not really pessimistic about this because I have every expectation that Clause 90 will be removed at committee stage. Therefore I would like to get this matter to committee at an early opportunity. Presumably, at that time, the Governments of the territories will have an opportunity to appear as witnesses. I think that this is really a technicality that can be put to rights with no great problem.
Finally, I would like to say that the territories have now come of age. Constitutional authority once granted to them is not to be rescinded. Here we are trying to rescind that authority under the guise of a Bill that deals with official languages. That is not acceptable to me or to my constituents. Therefore I hope that every consideration will be given to the remarks that I have made and to the remarks of other Members of the House of Commons speaking on the same issue when the Bill is referred to committee.
