Madam Speaker, I listened with care to the comments of the Hon. Member for Western Arctic (Mr. Nickerson). He has addressed an important matter felt quite keenly in the Northwest Territories. I would like to say something along a very similar line on behalf of the Government of the Yukon and in recognition of the fact that the Hon. Member for Yukon (Ms. McLaughlin) is not able to be here today. I know that she wanted to address a particular concern which is quite similar to the one which has just been put forward regarding the Northwest Territories.
We are concerned that the Bill be considered carefully in committee. We expect that it will soon go to committee. We are concerned that in Clause 3 of the Bill in which federal institutions are defined there is an exclusion, which is, of course, relevant to what the Hon. Member was just addressing. The definition of federal institution does not include any
March 7, 1988

institution of the Council or Government of the Northwest Territories. Because that particular exclusion is in place one might conclude that the Government of the Yukon, an institution of the Council or the Government of the Yukon, is in fact included under "federal institutions". That is a matter of grave concern to the Government of the Yukon. I think I can say that it is of grave concern to the entire Legislature and to all the people of that part of Canada.
This concern is very similar to the one expressed by the Hon. Member from the Northwest Territories and requires application here because the Yukon is practising full self-government. After the Meech Lake meeting the question of the Yukon, as with the Northwest Territories, achieving provincial status becomes profoundly problematic. That is one of the objectionable points that has been raised about the Meech Lake agreement.
It is proper that the Parliament of Canada should respect the Legislature, Council and Government of the Yukon and not impose on them official bilingualism but rather have them accept as we wish it to happen in the other provinces of Canada, the standing of English and French as official languages as is true in New Brunswick. We would like that to happen in other cases. The Government of the Yukon is advancing services and extending services and so on. But it is necessary at committee to take this up.
As the Hon. Member has anticipated, some revisions relating to the imposition of constraints on the Government of the Assembly of the Northwest Territories are essential. Similarly, there needs to be a recognition of this concern for the Yukon in the committee's consideration of the Bill.
I appreciate your allowing me the time, Madam Speaker, to put this case on behalf of the Yukon in the absence of the Hon. Member who is away on business elsewhere.

Madam Speaker, all I can say is that I agree with the comments of the Hon. Member. I did not speak of the Yukon in my address because I was not entirely clear what it is that the Government of the Yukon wants. It has not advised me of its particular standing on the issue. I would be pleased if it would be so kind as to do so.
When one looks at the Bill one sees that in many respects the Yukon has been treated even worse than the territories. The Government and the Legislature of the Yukon have been treated very much as a federal government Department in the Bill. I am sure that although the Government has not told me this, it would find that unacceptable.

Madam Speaker, I want to begin by commending my friend, the Hon. Member for Western Arctic (Mr. Nickerson), for drawing attention to the difficulties with respect to Clause 90. Toward the end of my remarks I wish to indicate my strong support for an amendment to that particular clause which in no way affects the principle of the Bill.
Official Languages Act
I am prepared to vote on the Bill, but my constituents would expect me, because of its great importance to French-speaking people outside Quebec, to express a strong word in favour of Bill C-72 which I consider to be an important Bill for Canada.
I consider it to be a necessary Bill. I consider it to be a piece of legislation which is in fact long overdue.
All of us here are aware that the Constitution of Canada provides that English and French be the official languages of Canada and have equality of status and equal rights and privileges as to their use in all of the institutions of Parliament and the Government of Canada.
However, the linguistic rights so guaranteed do not go far enough, in my view and certainly in the view of the Government and of the framers of the legislation, for example, in the area of the language of work. Hence there is a need for Bill C-72 which will serve to ensure respect for English and French as the official languages of Canada, especially in those areas in which there has been some difficulty in the recent past. I am thinking of the administration of justice. I am thinking of providing services to the public in all areas of Canada. I am thinking of carrying out the work of federal institutions in either one of the official languages.
Further than that, and most important to me and to the constituency in northern Ontario which I represent which has a significant Franco-Ontarian population, is one of the stated objects of Bill C-72. I refer to the support and the development of English and French linguistic minority communities and generally the advancement of the equality of status and use of the English and French languages within Canadian society.
Some Members of Parliament who keep abreast of these matters will know that in one of the major communities in my constituency, namely, Kapuskasing, there was in fact a struggle that finally ended up in the courts when the local council attempted to have the community designated as bilingual. In the end, because of the court decision, it had to pursue the goal of bilingualism in a somewhat different fashion. But had Bill C-72 been in place at the time, the cause of bilingualism would have been greatly strengthened.
Supporters of Canadian bilingualism will certainly hail and applaud this Bill. Bill C-72 bodes very well for the future of bilingualism in Canada. It builds on the very solid foundation that has been established by past Prime Ministers, including the Right Hon. John. G. Diefenbaker, the Right Hon. Lester B. Pearson, and, most particularly, the Right Hon. Pierre Elliott Trudeau.

With a view to strengthening federal legislation on the official languages, Bill C-72 has a three-fold objective: first to ensure the equality of the official languages, second to support the development of the official languages minorities and the advancement of equal status for both official languages and,

March 7, 1988
Official Languages Act
third, to define the powers and obligations of federal institutions with respect to this matter.

Clause 33 of Bill C-72 makes English and French the languages of work in all federal institutions. It grants to officers and employees of all federal institutions the right to use either of the official languages.
It has already been drawn to the attention of this House that the February issue of Western Report interprets this clause to mean that if a person is not bilingual then-

-you cannot work for the federal Government.

That, of course, is a gross misinterpretation. In that context, it does seem to me that a new generation of young Canadians is coming to realize that to be bilingual is a qualification which will assist enormously in promoting a career in the federal Public Service. The fact that many jobs now require fluency in both official languages should upset no one. In the same manner as mathematics is essential for engineering, chemistry is necessary to a career in pharmacy, and anatomy is required for medicine, it is increasingly recognized, if a person chooses a career in the Public Service of Canada at the federal level, that bilingualism is a prerequisite for that person to extend his or her career as far as his or her abilities will allow.
I was able to cut my political teeth on the policy of official bilingualism. 1 did so especially during the first Trudeau administration. I did so in all parts of the country where initially the policy was extremely unpopular. For example, I can remember on a radio call-in show where a man said to me that he was sick and tired of having French jammed down his throat. I asked him to elaborate a little, and he made reference to the famous cornflakes box. The conversation ended very abruptly when I told him that he was meant to eat the contents of the box, not the box itself.
Clause 40 of this Bill has particular appeal for me, and also for the Franco-Ontarian constituents whom I represent in this House. Under Clause 40 the federal Government is committed to enhancing the vitality of minority communities, supporting and assisting their development, and fostering the full recognition and use of both official languages.
It will be the task of Canada's Secretary of State (Mr. Crombie) to direct a co-ordinated approach to the implementation of this provision. Federal Ministers will be empowered by Bill C-72, if they are so designated by the Governor in Council or the Cabinet, to consult and negotiate with provincial Governments to ensure the co-ordination of federal, provincial, and municipal educational services in both official languages.
Canada's first Prime Minister said it as well as anyone. Sir John A. Macdonald, a Conservative Prime Minister, when
speaking to the House of Commons on February 17, 1890, as reported on page 745 of Hansard, stated:
I have no accord with the desire expressed in some quarters that by any mode whatever there should be an attempt made to oppress the one language or to render it inferior to the other; I believe that would be impossible if it were tried, and it would be foolish and wicked if it were possible.
Canada's first Prime Minister was correct. His statement, however, was made with a negative connotation. He spoke of the futility of repressing one language or the other in Canada.
Today, with Bill C-72, we are able to speak of the advancement of bilingualism, enhancing the vitality of English and French where it is necessary to do so, assisting the development of two official languages, and fostering their full recognition.
To the Party opposite, which now forms the Government of Canada, I can only say, "Congratulations. You have come a long way". In this legislation what the Government is doing is essentially right in every respect.
Henri Bourassa wrote this in 1916:
The preservation and simultaneous growth of two national languages-far from being an obstacle to the progress of Canada, constitutes its most powerful factor and our greatest national asset.
At this time we are only considering the principle of the Bill. There will be another time and occasion for a clause by clause analysis. With reference to one clause which I referred to earlier, I do wish to raise the need for an amendment. In advancing the cause of bilingualism, which I fully support, I fail to see why it is necessary to reduce the legislative authority of the Fegislative Assembly of the Northwest Territories. I refer to Clause 90 of Bill C-72 which prohibits that Legislature from amending one of its own statutes, namely, the Northwest Territories Official Languages Act, without the prior approval of the federal Parliament.
Hon. Members opposite will be quick to point out to me, as some have already done, that Clause 90 is consistent with an agreement reached between the then Secretary of State and the Government of the Northwest Territories on June 28, 1984. That is an agreement made by the previous Liberal Government.
I say to the House that such a provision was unnecessary then, and I further submit that paragraph 8, which put that obligation on the Legislative Assembly to seek permission from this Parliament, is no longer even in effect. The Bill which gave it effect, Bill C-26 of the day, died on the Order Paper.
All of that aside, we are now living in 1988. Despite the Meech Lake Accord which is a set-back for the North, the Legislative Assembly of the Northwest Territories is rapidly evolving toward full responsible Government. There is no agreement now in effect regarding official languages. The Northwest Territories has its own statute. Therefore, it is entirely logical and reasonable to argue that Clause 90 is not required.
March 7, 1988

Therefore, at a later stage in the consideration of this Bill, I will either move an amendment myself, or if the amendment comes from my friend, the Hon. Member for Western Arctic, I will support it. As I stated earlier, this in no way touches on the principle of this excellent piece of legislation.
I wish to conclude by commending the Government in general for bringing forward Bill C-72. I applaud its efforts, I welcome all aspects of this Bill, the thrust of it, and in particular I extend my congratulations to the Secretary of State who is responsible for the Bill.

I enjoyed listening to the Hon. Member. His address was positive. I believe some of the points he was raising are very important. For instance, the Bill does not require everybody to be bilingual. The Bill is based on the fact that there will always be English-speaking and Frenchspeaking unilingual people in this country. A second language is always advantageous, whether it is French, Ukrainian, Danish, Swedish, Chinese or whatever. There are Canadians today who speak two and three languages. There are others who never in a lifetime will want nor will there be a need for them to have a second language. Consequently, I think we have to make it very clear in our regulations and in the committee as it goes through this Bill that there will be no discrimination against unilinguals in the market-place where the work is done.
There is always the hope that people will be able to learn another language. As I mentioned this morning, the Government of Alberta is already encouraging people to learn the second official language. Some 23,000 students are enrolled in that program under the auspices of the Government of Alberta.
I would like the Hon. Member's comments. In the everyday working place that is wholly unilingual, the foreman, or the boss as he is sometimes called, should never be worried about the fact that he will not be promoted because he knows only one language, the one being the language of his working place. I think Canadians should be aware of that point and the committee should also cover it very carefully.
There is another point I would like to mention. I mention both points now to save time. The Hon. Member talked about federal institutions. He is right. This Bill does apply to federal institutions. Consequently, there is no reason at this time for people in provincial or municipal courts or provincial or municipal bodies to fear that someone will force them to speak a second language whether that language is French or English. I think that is a very important point we have to recognize.
The Bill is very important and the regulations and the administration of it are very important. I hope that when the Bill comes out of the committee it will be abundantly clear to all concerned that in a unilingual area there will be no pressure whatsoever placed on people forcing them to learn another language and that they will be able to have their promotions
Official Languages Act
on merit and ability. I would appreciate hearing the Hon. Member's comments.

Madam Speaker, I am pleased the Hon. Member for Bow River (Mr. Taylor) has raised that matter. The Bill itself takes account of the concern, the concern about the merit principle. In Clause 38 of the Bill in Part VI which deals with the language of work, it says quite clearly:
Nothing in this section shall be construed as abrogating or derogating from
the principle of selection of personnel according to merit.
I notice that the Hon. Member for Bow River was very precise in raising the point. He is talking about those areas where it is unnecessary to be bilingual, and in that area of the Public Service promotion should not be denied because a person does not have the capacity to speak both official languages. The Bill makes that perfectly clear. I think the Hon. Member from Bow River raised the point because I indicated to him that there is a growing number of positions in the federal service, certainly senior positions, in which bilingualism is required. I think I would continue to make it an appeal to the young people of Canada, and I know the young people in Alberta have responded very positively to it, that if they want a senior career or want to advance their career in the Public Service of Canada then bilingualism is one of the attributes they should have on their curriculum vitae. It will help them enormously.
It has now become commonplace to say that it is unthinkable that we would ever have a Prime Minister again in this country who is not fluently bilingual. If that is true for the Prime Minister of the country, it is true for many other senior positions in the Public Service, and the young people of the country will want to be cognizant of that. Having said that, however, the point made by the Hon. Member for Bow River is a valid one that where only one language is required, no one should be restricted from being promoted in a particular area.

Madam Speaker, it is with pleasure that I take part in the debate on Bill C-72 this afternoon. We are asked to consider Bill C-72 respecting the status and use of the official languages of Canada so as to promote respect for this country's linguistic duality. Madam Speaker, we need this piece of legislation to reaffirm our commitment respecting Canada's bilingualism policy. And even if there were no other reason to introduce Bill C-72, this reason in itself is enough to justify reaffirming this commitment in the House of Commons today. Of course, Madam Speaker, there are other reasons, and I will be dealing with them in the course of my remarks later this afternoon.
The first thing I want to say about this measure is: at last we are debating it in the House of Commons. I say "at last", Madam Speaker, because we have been waiting for two years to have this kind of measure. The Bill was introduced in the House on June 25, 1987 and promptly forgotten. Indeed the Hon. Member for Ottawa-Vanier (Mr. Gauthier) moved a non-confidence motion in the House on February 1 last to

March 7, 1988
Official Languages Act
denounce the Government's refusal to forge ahead with the official languages issue. Here is the text of the motion sponsored by my colleague the Hon. Member for Ottawa- Vanier:
That this House condemns the government for its inaction, its lack of political will and its hesitation to accept debate in the House of Commons, at the second reading stage, on Bill C-72 respecting the status and use of the official languages, thus causing a clear setback in the application of the Act by federal departments and agencies, in addition to having detrimental effects on national unity.
A hard-hitting motion, Madam Speaker, but still it did stir up some action: a few days later, on February 8, the House began the second reading debate on Bill C-72. It lasted two days and during that time seven Government Members and five opposition Members took the floor, hardly justification to claim that the measure has been debated at length in the House of Commons. Yet earlier today the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) took pleasure in blaming the Opposition for the snail-pace progress of this legislation. As he is wont to do, the Prime Minister takes it out on parliamentarians and other political Parties whenever he wants to hide his incompetence. We know better, Madam Speaker, we know that this measure has been at a standstill for two weeks and I would urge the Hon. Member for Chambly (Mr. Grise) to pay attention-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext: If the Prime Minister had spoken to this Bill you would still be making the same remarks.

-because he too has a lot to learn, Madam Speaker, a lot more than most other people, and if he listens carefully he just might learn something.
Finally, we have today this third day of debate in the House and, although the Prime Minister has chosen not to participate in it, he is to be blamed just the same for the lack of progress of the issue in the House. The two other political leaders, namely the Right Hon. Member for Vancouver Quadra (Mr. Turner) and the Hon. Member for Oshawa (Mr. Broadbent) have both participated in it. So far, the Prime Minister has refused to do so. I trust that he will honour us with his participation before this second reading debate comes to an end.
As I was saying, Madam Speaker, even if it were for no other reason than to reaffirm our commitment to the official languages issue, we should have Bill C-72 just the same. As 1 was saying, however, there are other reasons: first of all, since the original Official Languages Act was adopted, we have passed the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms and Sections 16 to 20 of the Charter dealing with the official languages issue. We have had also the Meech Lake Accord, so that we need to make a sort of new commitment and rejuvenate this legislation which is already several years old.
There had been several other previous initiatives which recognized the linguistic duality of this country so that the Official Languages Act is not the first. Think of the history of our country: The Quebec Act, 1774, made reference to the linguistic duality; The Union Act, 1840; The British North
America Act, 1867; and The Manitoba Act, 1870, even if this legislation was never or almost never enforced, and many others. Finally, let us not forget the Laurendeau-Dunton Report which gave birth to the present Official Languages Act. Naturally, this Laurendeau-Dunton Report was prepared at the request of the Right Hon. Lester B. Pearson, a former Primer Minister of Canada. In this Laurendeau-Dunton Report, the so-called Royal Commission of Inquiry on Bilingualism and Biculturalism in Canada concluded that our country needed an Official Languages Act to recognize in a concrete fashion the Canadian linguistic duality, as well as the need, privilege and right of every Canadian to be served by the Federal Government in the language of his or her choice.
Some have asked why we need a new Bill and why we need it now. We need it because it is finally time for us to revamp a law which has aged many years and because of the constitutional amendments we have made over recent decades including the Meech Lake constitutional Accord which has not yet been fully adopted and the 1982 constitutional document.

Madam Speaker, the Federation des francophones hors Quebec, in a press release dated February 4, deplores the Government's failure to act on the official languages issue, and I want to quote the following from the text released by the Federation:
What is the Mulroney Government waiting for? Why won't it proceed with
second and third reading of a Bill that was tabled six months ago? We can find
no explanation for the delay, and we want the Government to proceed
immediately.
Madam Speaker, it is clear Francophones outside Quebec are upset about the Conservative Government's failure to act. What does the Bill contain? I think it would be in order to give a brief enumeration of the main points of Bill C-72. First of all, the Bill will contain a preamble, defining the Government's commitments with respect to official languages. It will contain measures to provide for improved access to the administration of justice in both languages, a very important issue.
There will also be measures to improve the access to, and the direct visibility of, bilingual federal communications and services.
There are provisions recognizing the rights of Canadians to work in the official language of their choice in federal institutions, in accordance with the linguistic responsibility of these institutions.
There is also recognition of the principle of full participation by French-speaking and English-speaking Canadians in federal institutions.
There are many other measures, but I would like to conclude with what I consider to be a very important one, namely, the primacy of the rights and obligations of the future legislation
March 7, 1988

or this new Act over federal statutes that are not compatible with its provisions.
Madam Speaker, I have the honour of representing in the House the electoral district with the highest percentage of Francophones outside the province of Quebec.
There are about 70,000 Francophones in my riding, the electoral district of Glengarry-Prescott-Russell. The riding borders on Quebec, and as you know, Madam Speaker, since you cross my riding on your way to Ottawa, some parts of the riding border on Quebec to the north, east and south. So although we are in Ontario, we are almost surrounded by Quebec, which partly explains the high percentage of Francophones in my riding.
1 was born in Quebec and am a Franco-Ontarian by adoption, so I see myself as a Franco-Ontarian, as a Quebecer, but above all, as a French-speaking Canadian.

When we discuss the issue of official languages, it is important to bring to the attention of the House the commitment of the Government in that regard. One thing which has happened over the last few years which best describes to me what I believe is a lack of commitment on the part of the present Government was the trial of one Luc Paquette. Mr. Paquette asked the Court of Queen's Bench in Alberta for a French trial. He won the right to a French trial with a judge, jury and Crown Attorney. The federal Government appealed that decision to the Court of Appeal and challenged Mr. Paquette's right to the trial. Mr. Paquette ended up losing his right, though others who had made similar applications before were successful. Those who will make similar applications in the future, because of the precedent-setting decision in the Paquette case, will not be successful. I feel that that is an unfortunate move on the part of the Attorney General of Canada (Mr. Hnatyshyn), one which should not have been contemplated and one which this Government will live to regret.

We know, Madam Speaker, that many conservative members do not support the Official Languages Bill. To my knowledge, this is the only legislation since I came to this House that, despite unanimous support from Cabinet ministers and both opposition parties, does not enjoy the unanimous support of Government back-benchers.
We will soon see!

This is a very special situation, and a conservative member opposite is suggesting we will soon see. Indeed, Madam Speaker, we will see, first, whether Governe-ment members, who expressed such disagreement on the Bill, will be present to demand a division, since five members must rise to indicate their disapproval before there can be a division. Secondly, we will see whether there will be a division in this
Official Languages Act
House and whether hon. members will be present to vote in line with the views they expressed in this House in the past.
Let's get on with the vote now.

Once again, we hear from government Members who do not think that debating this issue is important. They have a right to think that. However, we have been debating this Bill for three days in the House of Commons, and for an inept Member to state otherwise is totally inaccurate. He should be ashamed of himself that such an important piece of legislation is being refused the opportunity to be debated.

Some will suggest, Madam Speaker, that the official languages Bill will force Canadians to be bilingual in order to work in the Public Service. I have here the February 1, 1988 copy of the Alberta Report, an English language magazine published in western Canada, and I would like to show it to you, but since this is contrary to our rules, I will simply read the cover which states:
Si vous ne pouvez pas lire ceci, vous ne pouvez pas travaiiler pour Ic
gouvernement federal.
Translation: "If you can't read this, you can't work for the federal Government".

Madam Speaker, we know that such a statement is totally inaccurate. We know that of the 221,000 jobs in the Public Service, 60 per cent require English only; 7 per cent, French only, and 28 per cent are designated bilingual.
How is it then possible to utter such nonsense, suggesting that if a Canadian is not totally bilingual he or she cannot work in the Public Service? This is absolutely false, as most hon. members in this House know.

Earlier this year there was an election in the Province of Ontario which, of course, was won in a landslide by the Liberal Party. In that election one political Party chose to fight the election against bilingualism and, in my opinion, on the backs of French Canadians in Ontario.
This political Party, supported by an outfit calling itself APEC, the so-called Alliance for the Preservation of English in Canada, was going from constituency to constituency trying to convince municipalities to adopt resolutions declaring themselves officially unilingual. In my opinion those resolutions were reprehensible, and luckily only a few municipalities fell for that trap set by APEC and the issue went nowhere. However, the general theme was picked up by the provincial leader of the Conservative Party and that Party was just about wiped out in the election.

March 7, 1988
Western Economic Diversification Act
There was a message in that, the message being that Canadians have now evolved beyond that. If such schemes ever worked, they will not work in 1988. I am sure that the present federal Government has realized that and I hope that it will assist in their decision some of the back-benchers who had some reservations about the Bill.
You haven't convinced anybody.

Madam Speaker, it is not important that I convince anyone. What is important is that the people of Canada have an Official Languages Act which is in their interest and will reflect the fact that we live in 1988, not that we are vestiges of the former century, as some Members of this House would like us to be.
I will conclude by reminding this House that the Mayor of Alexandria, a town in my constituency, said not long ago that APEC should stand for "All People Created Equal".

All Canadians are equal. All Canadians have equal rights. We will know in a few moments whether Government back-benchers will have the courage to express their convictions, whether they will rise in this House to demand a division to determine whether members support or reject Bill C-72. I hope we will enact the Bill. Naturally, as anyone else I wish for amendments, improvements, but a vast majority in this House will support Bill C-72 today, and we will send it to a committee of the House. But Bill C-72 must not die in that committee! We must discuss the matter, we must discuss it rapidly, and bring it back in this House to enact it in order that Canada in 1988 may have an Official Languages Act, 1988.

ADVISABILITY OF ESTABLISHING A NATIONAL FOOD POLICY Mr. Steven W. Langdon (Essex-Windsor) moved:
That, in the opinion of this House, the Government should consider the advisability of establishing an improved national marketing structure for all major farm produced commodities and negotiate with the provinces a national food policy with over-all production targets and market sharing.
He said: Madam Speaker, last Friday night I attended the Essex County Federation of Agriculture annual meeting to honour their activities. I found myself sitting opposite two young people who had been working since they entered the labour force to try to earn enough to provide some kind of basis on which they could purchase a farm. They came from farming families and wanted to establish a future in farming for themselves. This motion is very much directed at them and toward hundreds of farmers across my constituency with whom I have talked in the last three and a half years.
Frankly, they have faced very difficult circumstances throughout that three and a half year period. The two young people I faced last Friday should be the future of our farming community, yet that young woman and man had found themselves in a position where the prospect of getting into farming, rather than becoming a more realistic goal, was becoming less likely, despite the fact they were earning more and saving more money.
I suggest that this is just one sign of the reality of the farm crisis which exists across Canada. The farm crisis in Essex County and in many other parts of Canada can be seen in terms of the very heavy debt loads which farmers are carrying. The crisis in Essex County is shown by a drop from one-third to two-fifths in the price of land which farmers have held for the last four to six years. The consequence of this to a farmer who has contracted a very significant debt is that the asset which covers that debt is very much reduced year by year.
National Food Policy
However, the heart of the crisis is not the debt load which farmers carry. As the Essex County Federation of Agriculture told the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) in a letter: "Despite highly efficient agricultural operations the current prices for farm commodities do not cover the basic costs of production in many cases, do not provide any return on investment, nor a reasonable wage for labour expended plus management skills".
In addition, as I have suggested in the House on a number of occasions, there are various mechanisms of harassment which Governments seem to be using to undercut farmers' potential for the future. For instance, one has seen in Essex County a doubling in the tax audits affecting farmers in the past year. Much tougher definitions are being applied in the process of this auditing, which has the effect of putting the farmer in a catch 22 situation. He or she must go out to find a job off farm in order to cover debts and the low prices for commodities, then tax audits refuse to classify this farmer as a full-time farmer because of the job he or she has had to take off farm. The consequence is that they are able to write off much less of their losses than was true previously.
Of course, farmers are not just sitting back and taking this. Farmers across Essex County and right across the country are fighting back with imaginative approaches and new methods of organization.
Again, to use my own constituency of Essex-Windsor, as an example the National Farmers' Union has formed a new local within the county which has expanded tremendously. One of the methods it is using to fight back is to hire people with an accounting background to go to the various Farm Debt Review Boards, which are held to look at the farmers who have got into difficult debt positions, and through the National Farmers' Union could work out as effective and optimistic a picture of the farm operation under scrutiny as is possible.
The union has been quite successful in a number of cases in persuading both Farm Debt Review Boards and banks that farms which appeared at first glance to be non-viable, with some satisfactory writing down of debt, some sort of sharing of the debt burden-for which farmers are not responsible-are really viable. It is not farmers who raised interest rates to 22 per cent in the early 1980s. Yet they are the people who are having to carry the burden of this increase.
The National Farmers' Union has fought back on that level. The Essex County Federation of Agriculture has fought back on the question of prices and the lack of relationship between prices and the cost of production for most farmers. Our office in the last few days has been talking with various experts in the farm community in Essex County. They have been able to generate figures which give one a sense of the depth of the crisis. The cost of production of soybeans is about $6.08 per

National Food Policy
bushel. The soybean growers' estimate of what they will receive as a price is $6.42 per bushel. It is at least some positive return, but a very small one. The cost of production of soft winter white wheat, another major crop in Essex County, is estimated at $3.19 per bushel. The market price as of today is $3.45 per bushel. Most farmers would have delivered their wheat in August of 1987, at which point the price was $3 per bushel. They would have lost something in the order of 19 cents to 20 cents per bushel with respect to their soft winter white wheat.
Perhaps the most hardest hit of commodities in my county is corn. The cost of production is approximately $3.18 per bushel. The market price is $2.02. The loss is over one dollar per bushel for these farmers.
What can we do when we are faced with these prices? I think it is something that has to concern all of us in this House. It is why I have tried on as many occasions as I could to speak out about these farm concerns. I think the first thing we have to do is to look at our marketing structures throughout this country. With respect to dairy farmers, with the feather industry, it has become viable, for the most part, to be a farmer, because there is successful supply management which works well. I speak with some personal experience on this subject. My family has operated a dairy farm north of Guelph very successfully since the period that supply management came in. So it has worked and it has worked with the feather industry.
Poultry farms are successful now and would not have been in the past. I recognize it is more complex for crops which are exported rather than serving the domestic market, as is the case, for the most part, with dairy products and the feather industry. However, with respect to those export crops, it is possible to have a two-price system. We have had it with respect to wheat quite successfully. One of my great sorrows with respect to the trade deal which has been presented by the Government to us in the House is that the two-price system for wheat is going to disappear. With respect to the two-price wheat system, the Ontario Wheat Board stated that Canada's two-price wheat policy has been a very important stabilizing factor in the general domestic wheat industry. The pricing mechanism provided by the policy has worked well for both the marketing board and the millers. Supplies have been assured and purchase risks have been eliminated through established prices to millers and processors.
It is not just processors; consumers as well have a predictable price. They do not see these jumps and ups and downs which have taken place in many farm commodities, which make it hard to predict. So they have a world for which they have been able to budget and which they understand. I think it is absolutely crucial that we have an improved marketing structure for all major farm produced commodities. It will have to be negotiated with the provinces. It will have to involve a national food policy, not just provincial food policies. We will have to accept over-all production targets and market sharing within our domestic market. Of course, we have to accept as a
reality also that for exports we cannot apply that kind of price predictability. We have to accept that those ups and downs are going to take place.
We have to negotiate with the provinces for the fullest possible coverage, for help for starting farmers. We have to deal with some of the problems, which, I admit, have existed with respect to national marketing structures, including the accelerated cost of quotas which have prevented some young farmers from getting into farming.
The last word I want to leave with the House is that besides the points made in this motion I stress that it is crucial that we keep in Canada the capacity to direct our own affairs with respect to agricultural policy. That is why I find the free trade proposal of the Government, the trade deal with the United States, to be so destructive with respect to many parts of agriculture, specifically those parts of agriculture that I represent in my constituency.

Madam Speaker, I am pleased to be able to join in this debate in Private Member's Hour on the motion raised by the Hon. Member for Essex-Windsor (Mr. Langdon).
The Hon. Member has touched on problems which are certainly common to agriculture across the country and which I think relate specifically to the grains and oilseeds sector which has been beset by low prices as a result of conditions in the market-place lying beyond the borders of our country. Of course, I am talking about the trade war between the United States and the European Economic Community. This is a problem which has been discussed countless times in the House. I do not think it needs revisiting at this point in time.
The question is what to do about it. Of course, a number of initiatives have been taken by the Government which I intend to enlarge upon later in my remarks.
First, I want to say in response to the Hon. Member's remarks that, certainly, there is an enormous overhang of farm debt out there. We are told right now that there is something in the order of $22 billion owing against farms in Canada. It is worth noting that the Standing Committee on Agriculture at this time is embarking upon a study of that very problem. It is called the "22 billion dollar problem". It is intended to try to seek some solutions to this overhang of farm debt resulting from the overcapitalization of agriculture during a period of rampant inflation followed by the catastrophic drop in grain and oil seed prices.
The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Clark) seconded the Hon. Member's motion. The Parliamentary Secretary has asked me to indicate that he did so, not out of support for the intent of the motion, but because in the absence of any opposition Member in the House at that time he wanted the Member's motion to be heard. It was for that reason that he seconded the motion.
March 7, 1988

The Hon. Member for Essex-Windsor talked about domestic wheat pricing, the two-price wheat policy, as some sort of argument in favour of the thrust of his motion that the Government consider further supply management schemes relative, I gather, to the grain sector. Frankly, I found that rather curious. There is no question that the domestic wheat benefit, the two-price wheat system, is being phased out at this time, not as a result of anything relating to the trade agreement between Canada and the United States but, rather, to the distorting influences which that artificial program has had on production and cropping patterns across Canada over the past several years.
In that regard I want to refer the Hon. Member to the report of the Special Committee on the Pricing of Domestic Wheat which reported to the House in the spring of 1986. That was an all-Party committee which travelled across the country. It listened to the interests of farm groups, producers, Governments and food processors. It concluded that there were problems relating to the policy. In particular it related to the fact that it was already leading to a distortion and a displacement of production in the sense that an artificial price of $6 or $7 per bushel of wheat would tend to encourage a tremendous movement into that kind of production in areas where, traditionally, other crops had been grown. Over the past two years we have seen the problems that that committee flagged becoming exacerbated.
As the Hon. Member has pointed out, the result is that in Ontario there has been a tremendous movement into the production of hard wheat, which traditionally has not been grown there, with a consequent displacement of that domestic wheat benefit and a shift in it from western Canada into Ontario and, indeed, into other areas of the country. I think that has caused considerable difficulties. It perhaps points out one of the problems relating to the sort of policy which has the capability of sending the wrong signals into the market-place, distorting production and sending producers chasing after something that is artificial. I think it has caused a problem.
In any event, I want to assure the House that the Government well knows the importance of agriculture to the country. It recognizes the enormous contribution that agriculture makes to our economy. It well understands that it has a responsibility to ensure that agriculture has a strong and stable future.
It is important to be clear about this responsibility. I do not believe it is up to the Government to impose marketing systems that Canadian farmers neither need nor want. What the Government must do is to continue to work with the provinces and with the private sector to develop effective long-term plans. That is exactly what it is doing at this time. The national agriculture strategy signed by the federal and provincial Ministers of Agriculture in the fall of 1986 is a major milestone in federal-provincial relations.
At that meeting the Ministers agreed that the long-term future of the agri-food industry depends upon maintaining existing markets, developing new markets and responding to
National Food Policy
changes in the domestic and international environment. It depends on effective measures to address farm income problems.
Regulated marketing can be an important part of the solution. Supply management has certainly helped to provide stable incomes to producers in certain sectors, particularly the dairy, poultry and egg sectors. The policy of the Government and of the Progressive Conservative Party has been to look to producer choice in those particular sectors. If the bulk of producers want that form of program, it has been the policy of the Government to attempt to assist. In that regard I cite the establishment of the Canadian Broiler Hatching Egg Agency in 1986 during the term of this Government.
There is no question that supply management can be effective in certain sectors, notably ones that 1 think would have difficulty in the international market, those sectors which traditionally have not been exporters. Of course, it was the producers themselves who asked for the authority to establish national marketing plans in these areas. It was the producers themselves who helped to bring their own supply management systems about.
Producers in many other sectors simply do not consider supply management to be a viable solution. I cite cattle and hog producers who are strongly opposed to production targets and to market shares. Although the issue is raised repeatedly, a majority of red meat producers have rejected consistently supply management as being incompatible with their marketing goals. Our red meat industry competes successfully in the international market-place exporting much of what it produces.
Another example of course is the grains and oilseeds sector in which production targets and market sharing run against the current consensus among grain and oil seed producers and their organizations. The fact is that fully 80 per cent of our production of wheat, for example, goes into the international market-place. Clearly, with that kind of emphasis on export it is impossible to apply any sort of suggestion such as the Hon. Member has made relative to that sector.
I see that my time is almost up. I wish to reiterate that the Government recognizes the crisis caused by the international trade war in the grains and oilseeds sector. It has come forward with programs of historical magnitude in terms of assistance to the grains and oilseeds producers, including huge payments under western grain stabilization, two successive Canadian special grains programs, fuel tax rebates, and a myriad of other programs to help tide the grain producers over this time of crisis.
On the international scene, various Ministers, including the Minister of State for Grains and Oilseeds (Mr. Mayer), through the Cairns Group have been actively pursuing attempts to bring a measure of sanity back into the international market-place. Indeed, this week the Minister of State

for Grains and Oilseeds returned from Argentina after another round of talks to attempt to reduce the effects of subsidies world-wide which have had the effect of causing these disastrous prices to our producers.
I congratulate the Hon. Member for again flagging the problem. It gives us an opportunity here to point out that some of it is caused by factors beyond our borders, but Government is responding to it in a measure which is unparalleled in Canadian history.

Madam Speaker, I am happy to have an opportunity to say a few words on the motion put forward by the Hon. Member for Essex-Windsor (Mr. Langdon). Agricultural marketing is perhaps the most difficult and challenging responsibility for farmers and Governments across the country in the whole agricultural production question.
We are very capable, particularly in the developed countries of the world, of producing massive amounts of food. The question is, how can we market those products both domestically and internationally at a price that is adequate to give the farmer a decent return on his investment?
We have seen the chaos created by the United States with its Farm Bill and with the massive subsidy program, which is not only designed to drive down the price of food, especially grains and cash crop items, but at the same time guarantee its own producers a very reasonable level of return. At the same time as the United States is driving down the world price, it has been providing massive export subsidies to its markets. It has been estimated that it has driven the price down by approximately $3 billion and provided some $6 billion or $8 billion per year in compensation to its producers.
This total chaos has been the greatest challenge ever faced by Canadian agriculture. No piece of legislation in the history of our country, in this Legislature or in any other, has had such a devastating impact on Canadian agriculture. Thousands and thousands of farmers have been put out of business because of the international trade wars which are now going on between the United States and the European Economic Community.
The disturbing part is that perhaps those trade wars are not finished. At some stage in the next year or two we hope that the United States and the EEC will draw back. Although the funding is only for three years, the American Bill provides for the legislation being in place for five years. If the funding continues and no international agreements are made, then the same chaos will continue.
We have seen a dramatic rise in the number of farmers in our country who are facing bankruptcy. It has risen from
30,000	or 32,000 to approximately 50,000 farmers who are either in serious financial difficulty or who are totally insolvent. The Government has not responded. Over one year ago the FCC went into a lack of financial viability. The Government has not responded by providing funding to take FCC out
of its state of insolvency. On April 30, 1987 that was estimated at $124 million, and the estimates are that by the end of this fiscal year it will be up to $300 million. It is clear that the situation for many farmers is untenable with regard to the farm debt crisis.
The situation of extremely low world prices, farm debt brought on by devaluation in farm land, put in context with the uncertainty of the whole supply managed market for the dairy and poultry industries, for the fruit and vegetable industry, for the grape industry, and for many other industries, by the free trade deal with the United States, has caused either the greatest financial instability, in the case of supply management managed commodities, or the greatest uncertainty which our country has ever seen in agriculture.
The free trade deal will cause immediate violent repercussions in some areas, for example, in the production of grapes. Our grape producers in the Okanagan Valley and the Niagara Escarpment have input costs of $600 to $800 a tonne for grapes, competing with grapes produced in the southern areas of California at $100 to $200 a tonne. This is simply not viable. That whole industry is facing a colossal disaster, an agricultural and industrial adjustment of tremendous proportions, yet there is no provision in the free trade agreement for that. Simply put, they have been sacrificed. They know it. They have been promised there would be a phase-out or adjustment period of 10 years. There is no adjustment period of 10 years; it is cold turkey next January, if the deal is passed.
The deal may not be passed. The United States Congress may well turn it down. The United States Congress may well require that the Government of Canada fulfil its commitment in the trade deal to ensure that the provinces will comply. The Government stated it would do that. There is no known way that that can be done, unless the Government invokes the peace, order, and good government clause, the emergency stand-by powers of the Constitution. As I understand it, the Government has stated it will not invoke those sections of the Constitution in order to implement the trade deal, so the deal may fall apart because of that. It may fall apart because of a general election. But at this stage we have to assume that the Government, having 210 Members of Parliament, will likely pass the enabling legislation.
The whole range of agricultural commodities will face the problems of the free trade deal, including canola meal and canola oil, which have found a tremendous market in the Pacific northwest, where it will be subjected to the loss of transportation assistance under the Western Grain Transportation Act. It is expected they will lose some $30 or $35 a tonne for transportation under the free trade deal, whereas the tariffs which apply to canola meal and to canola oil going to the Pacific Northwest running as high as over $30 a tonne will not be viable for them. It is just the same with fruit and vegetables. The growers have operated under the protection of seasonal tariffs. If they are an expanding industry, those tariffs are removed. The snap-back provision, which is in the Act and often hailed by the Government, is not in fact available.

Without getting into all of the commodities, Madam Speaker, you can see that the free trade deal with the United States will have an extremely adverse effect on the marketing of a number of commodities. The commodities are simply not viable when put into direct competition with low-priced commodities coming in from the United States at uncontrolled levels and price.

Madam Speaker, I am pleased to enter into this debate on the motion presented by the Hon. Member for Essex-Windsor (Mr. Langdon), who is proposing that we have a national food policy with production targets and market shares for all major farm commodities. He is suggesting that we have supply management for industries that depend greatly on export. If we followed his suggestion, we would lose 35 per cent of all the pork producers in Canada. One in three, every third person down the road, would be out of business. If we followed his suggestion, we would have 80 per cent of the wheat producers in Canada out of business and 12 per cent of the beef producers. The Member is suggesting that we can find some way to have both supply management and an export market, but I do not think that is at all possible and the end result will be as I have already said.
The Canadian Consumers Association emphasized that point and the producers in the dairy, poultry and egg sectors have benefited greatly from the supply management schemes that are in place at the present time. Other countries have not had these programs and they have paid through massive export subsidies, subsidies which the Hon. Member for Algoma (Mr. Foster) spoke about as disrupting farm income in Canada, and, indeed, in North America. The Americans have had to do something by trying to buy down the excess dairy cattle. This happened in the United States last year and in the European Economic Community before. Certainly supply management has cost Canadian consumers a small amount, but they have a good and high quality product on a regular basis and consumers and producers have been well served.
This Government is fully supportive of supply management schemes. In fact, we have, since we came into power, brought in the latest of the supply management schemes through a national marketing agency for broiler hatching eggs which was created in 1986. Supply management is not the panacea for the entire agricultural industry. It is important that we recognize that the agricultural industry is very diverse and that what works in one sector indeed will not necessarily work in another sector or may perhaps be unnecessary in another sector. That is why the Government has made a commitment to producers that we will support whatever marketing systems producers decide work best for their particular commodities, as long as those interests are also in the public interest. Some commodity sectors believe that they are better off with a free market system. Most red meat producers, for instance, are opposed to supply management.
National Food Policy
In 1986, beef producers in this country earned cash receipts of $3.6 billion. Of this amount, more than $413 million came from exports of beef and beef products. This is the amount the Hon. Member for Essex-Windsor would be prepared to sacrifice for a supply management scheme. Hog producers reported cash receipts of $2.1 billion. Exports accounted for more than $800 million of this amount. Again, this is the amount that would be sacrificed. Red meat exports earned more than $1.2 billion for the Canadian economy. That is more than $1.2 billion toward a favourable trade balance. Canada simply cannot afford to produce red meat exclusively for the domestic market. The red meat sector is certainly among the healthiest parts of the Canadian farm economy.
When dairy, poultry and egg producers opted for the supply management system, it was to bring order out of chaos. Their sectors had been ravaged by boom and bust cycles that cost them and Canadians a great deal. They sought some sort of orderly marketing to provide stability to their sectors. Red meat producers prefer unfettered markets, and they are managing quite well. What is more, contrary to what the Member for Algoma has just said, red meat producers are excited by their prospects under the free trade agreement. They anticipate increased export opportunities under free trade with the United States. This would be lost under a supply-managed scheme.
Many farm sectors will benefit from the removal of tariffs and the elimination of technical barriers, but perhaps none more so than the red meat sector. Stan Wilson, President of the Canadian Cattlemen's Association, has said free trade is welcomed by cattle producers right across the country. Bill Vaggs, head of the Canadian Pork Council, said he is "very comfortable" with the free trade agreement. He has urged the federal Government to do everything in its power to keep the doors open to the United States market for Canada's hog and pork exports.
Even the report by the Ontario Ministry of Agriculture and Food, a ministry headed by a person dedicated to finding reasons why free trade is bad for Ontario agriculture, even that department working under that kind of direction failed to find a problem for the read meat sector. In fact, it found that there would be some $18 million advantage per year in Ontario alone for the red meat sector. This same study, I believe, forgot that farmers are consumers and consume a great deal of products in their farm operation and would benefit from a reduction in tariffs and the products which they consume. It also failed to realize that many farmers have children, even farmers themselves who work off the farm and would benefit from more jobs that pay higher in their communities. The very least optimistic report which the Ontario Government could find still showed an $18 million advantage for Ontario red meat producers.
In recent years, the value of Canadian red meat and live animal exports to the United States has totalled more than $1 billion a year, nearly half of Canada's farm exports to that country. Our red meat sector is fully competitive with the U.S.

National Food Policy
Its assured duty free access to the U.S. market helps guarantee the continued well-being of this sector.
The free trade agreement will exempt both our countries from each other's meat import laws. Without an agreement, U.S. meat import law could limit Canada's beef and veal exports to the United States, either through formal import quotas or so-called voluntary export restraints. The agreement is going to provide an improved environment for additional investment in meat processing plants since there is now much greater certainty of continued access to the U.S. market. That, of course, demonstrates again the tendency for years where we in Canada have sent more money out of this country across the border to invest in American business to avoid tariffs, money that could have stayed here at home to produce Canadian jobs. Of course, the more money we keep at home, the greater the chance for Canadian employment.
The particular advantage that Canadian meat producers will have will be the removal of the tariffs on portion-controlled cuts of high quality beef. This should provide a greatly increased market in the United States.
The trade deal also addressed the broadest possible package of mutually beneficial trade barrier reductions, an end to the misuse of technical barriers in such areas as meat inspection where every lot could have been inspected as it went across the border, and the misuse of food additives as well as the use of specific veterinary drugs will facilitate red meat export. How well the pork industry knows of the problem with chloram-phenical, indeed, the long-lasting problem of chloramphenical which is not presently available to the Canadian producer. Red meat producers have every reason to be optimistic about their prospects under free trade and every reason to be optimistic about their industry's future.
The motion before us today is not new. Back in 1971, beginning with Bill C-176 it was proposed that we establish the Farm Products Marketing Agencies Act. Originally, cattle and hogs were covered under this Act. A very spirited defence from a variety of organizations fought over a year and had the red meat sector excluded. Since that time the issue has resurfaced on many occasions and is resurfacing in the Ontario sector on a regular basis through the Federation of Agriculture. Some individuals favour supply management for red meat. However, the majority of the industry is clearly not in support of this alternative.
In 1986, at a national workshop on hog marketing alternatives, Canada's pork producers turned thumbs down on supply management. There are certainly viable alternatives, however, for the industry. These would include tripartite stabilization plans, the new commodity type mortgages under the Farm Credit Corporation and the Farm Debt Review Agency about which the Hon. Member for Essex-Windsor talked.
The red meat industry is not asking for supply management. Without any sort of regulated intervention in the marketplace, the red meat industry is competing with vigour and with success. There are better methods of supporting the industry, methods that I outlined briefly above, and that is the course this Government will take.

Madam Speaker, it gives me great pleasure to join in the balance of the debate on Motion No. 99 presented by the Hon. Member for Essex-Windsor (Mr. Langdon) calling for the establishment of an improved national marketing strategy for all major farm-produced commodities and for the negotiation with the provinces of a national food policy with over-all production targets and market sharing.
I think some Hon. Members who have spoken, particularly those on the government side, seem to have taken this motion somewhat out of context. They immediately say that this is an attempt to set up supply-managed marketing for all commodities across Canada. That is not necessarily so. It is an attempt to discuss with the provinces a long-term national marketing strategy.
This motion is timely because of the circumstances in which we live. We have seen develop over the last four or five years an income crisis in agriculture as farm returns do not meet the cost of production. This has in turn augmented a debt crisis so $22 billion to $23 billion-worth of debt is now being carried by Canada's farmers, a debt load which they cannot afford to carry, given the current value of land and the market outlook.
We have watched as land and agricultural assets have deteriorated in value. There has been deflation in the agricultural sector for the last five years, yet the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) is still attempting to fight inflation. In rural areas across Canada, land values are between 40 per cent and 50 per cent lower than they were four or five years ago. Yet the Minister persists in trying to fight what he calls inflation. To do that, he has kept the interest rate higher than it needs to be. It is 1.25 per cent higher this year than it was a year ago. This has meant high fixed rates for Farm Credit Corporation loans. These rates are so high that the very small amount of money the Government made available for the FCC to lend was not even taken up by farmers. They went elsewhere to get loans at much cheaper rates.
Because the Government persists in holding the interest rate higher than it needs to be in order to fight inflation in the Toronto area, the Canadian dollar has risen to the 79-cent level from about 71 cents or 72 cents in the past year. This means that for farmers who export, the price of their commodities has effectively fallen 10 to 12 per cent and the cost of borrowing money has risen 1 per cent to 1.25 per cent.
A bit over a year ago, the agriculture committee took it upon itself to investigate ways of reducing costs at the farm gate and attempted to look at the price of inputs and what could be done by Government and farmers to reduce those input costs. We found that there was not very much that could be done in terms of real savings, which would have meant more
March 7, 1988

money in farmers' pockets. Very little could be achieved. There has been virtual free trade in farm chemicals and most farm inputs including farm machinery. The trade deal would not solve that problem and has not solved that problem. It may have exacerbated some other problems on the market side, but I will deal with that later.
The only hope farmers have of having a bottom line that leaves money in their pockets is in doing something about the marketing end. In a number of commodities, farmers have turned their attention to that in the past, and I will review very quickly, because I see that time is short, the three methods farmers have utilized to improve their bargaining power in the market over the past 50 or 60 years.
During the First World War, the Canadian Wheat Board was first established as a single-desk seller of all western Canadian wheat. The farmers hated it. There was a great political furore when the Government set up that Wheat Board. In fact, the political impetus for setting it up, going back in history, was that the grain traders on the grain exchange had got themselves into a box they could not get out of, so the Government intervened, froze all the assets and began marketing the grain itself. The grain traders had sold four, five and six times as much grain as actually existed and there was no way that contracts could be met.
After a year's experience with the board, farmers began to see the advantage of single-desk selling. They got a higher price for that crop of grain than they had ever received before. They got an even price, regardless of when they were able to deliver. They all got the same price, and they decided that they liked that. There is no way now that farmers would give up that single-desk selling agency, the Canadian Wheat Board, which markets export grain at the moment and has been undermined a bit over the years.
Another type of single-desk agency is provincial hog marketing boards, one of which I was active in setting up in the Province of Saskatchewan. They function like little wheat boards with less bargaining power because they restrict themselves to their own bailiwick. If they were able to get together across the nation and market through one desk nationally, they would be able to extract another one cent, two cents or three cents per pound for hogs from the various processing firms. That is an option that is held back from them by the current legislation which does not permit any commodity to put together that kind of a national program except those that are named in the legislation including dairy products, poultry, eggs, now tobacco and soon, I hope, potatoes.
The third type of system is the type everyone hates, everyone on the government side at least, and that is the supply managed marketing boards, which work very well and are the epitome of efficiency in commodities that are very necessary for the maintenance of good food and nutrition. They have done a good job of providing consumers with exactly the amount needed without producing waste which only adds to

the cost and is an unnecessary expense to the system. I regret to see that my time is up, Madam Speaker.
